title: The Whiting Paper Mill Explosion
summary: In 1888, the George A. Whiting Paper Company mill in Menasha exploded and burned. The disaster destroyed the mill, and the operation was rebuilt at the site.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — George A. Whiting Paper Company

title: Menasha Wooden Ware Became an Industrial Giant
summary: The Menasha Wooden Ware Company grew from an earlier pail-making business into a nationally important manufacturer of tubs, pails, barrels, broom handles, clothespins and other wooden products. By the early twentieth century, its Menasha operations covered dozens of buildings.
source: Wisconsin Labor History — Menasha Corporation historical bibliography

title: A Massive Fire Changed Menasha Wooden Ware
summary: A major fire on July 17, 1964 destroyed the longtime Menasha headquarters plant of the Menasha Wooden Ware Corporation. The company later relocated its main operations to nearby Neenah.
source: Wisconsin Labor History — Menasha Corporation historical bibliography

title: The Hill of the Dead
summary: Near Little Lake Butte des Morts stood a mound remembered as the Hill of the Dead. The place became associated with conflict involving the Meskwaki, or Fox, people and French forces in the eighteenth century.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Hill of the Dead in Butte des Morts

title: A Fox Village Once Stood Near Here
summary: Historical maps and later surveys document a Meskwaki, or Fox, settlement in the Butte des Morts area. French military expeditions moved through this region during conflicts with the Fox people in the early eighteenth century.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Butte des Morts historical maps

title: Neenah Was Once Known as Winnebago Rapids
summary: Before the name Neenah became established, the settlement was known as Winnebago Rapids. Its location on the Fox River helped attract flour mills, lumber businesses and eventually the paper industry.
source: Wisconsin Digital Collections — Neenah Local History Collection

imageAlt: Historic depiction of the 1871 Peshtigo Fire
title: The Deadliest Fire in American History
summary: On October 8, 1871, a firestorm swept through Peshtigo and northeastern Wisconsin. In only hours, entire communities were destroyed and roughly 1,500 people were killed. The catastrophe occurred the same night as the Great Chicago Fire but was far deadlier.

imageAlt: Historic Ringling Brothers Circus winter quarters in Baraboo, Wisconsin
title: The Greatest Show on Earth Started Here
summary: The Ringling brothers launched their circus from Baraboo in 1884 as a small wagon show with no menagerie or wild animals. Within decades, their operation had grown into the largest circus empire in the United States.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Ringling Brothers Circus Winter Quarters

imageAlt: Wisconsin State Capitol after the 1904 fire in Madison
title: Wisconsin's Capitol Burned to the Ground
summary: Early on February 27, 1904, fire broke out inside Wisconsin's State Capitol. Firefighters battled the blaze for about 18 hours, but nearly the entire building was destroyed. Governor Robert La Follette helped rescue government records from the burning structure.

title: Why Wisconsin Is Called the Badger State
summary: Thousands of miners poured into southwestern Wisconsin during the lead boom. Some lived in crude shelters dug directly into hillsides. Their underground homes earned the miners the nickname 'badgers' — a name that eventually became associated with Wisconsin itself.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Lead Mining in Southwestern Wisconsin

title: Oshkosh Became 'Sawdust City'
summary: Oshkosh became one of America's great lumber centers during the nineteenth century. After the Great Chicago Fire created enormous demand for building materials, Oshkosh mills helped supply the rebuilding effort. By 1873 the city had 24 sawmills and became known as 'Sawdust City.'
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — A Brief History of Oshkosh

title: The Final Massacre of the Black Hawk War
summary: Near the mouth of the Bad Axe River, hundreds of Sauk men, women and children attempting to cross the Mississippi were trapped by U.S. troops and a gunboat. The killings on August 1 and 2, 1832 ended the Black Hawk War and remain one of the darkest episodes in Wisconsin's early history.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Battle of Bad Axe

title: Milwaukee Became a Beer Capital
summary: German immigration, abundant water, ice, grain and transportation helped transform Milwaukee into one of America's great brewing cities. By the 1890s Milwaukee breweries were producing millions of barrels of beer and the industry had become inseparable from the city's identity.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Brewing and Prohibition

title: Cornish Miners Built a Little Piece of England
summary: The lead boom brought experienced miners from Cornwall, England, to Mineral Point. They built distinctive limestone cottages using traditions carried across the Atlantic. Many survive today, giving parts of Mineral Point an appearance unlike almost anywhere else in Wisconsin.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Mineral Point Historic District

title: A Shipwreck Still Lies Beneath Lake Michigan
summary: The schooner F.J. King was built in 1867 to haul cargo across the Great Lakes and was designed to squeeze through the Welland Canal locks with only inches to spare. After sinking off Door County, its wreck remained beneath Lake Michigan and is now recognized as a historic archaeological site.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — F.J. King Shipwreck

title: Superior's Waterfront Moved Mountains of Iron
summary: Massive ore docks along Superior's waterfront connected Midwestern mines with Great Lakes freighters. Elevated rail lines carried ore above waiting ships, where it could be dumped into their holds and transported east through the Great Lakes industrial network.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Ore Docks, Superior

title: The Bay View Massacre
summary: National Guard troops fired on workers marching for the eight-hour day in Bay View during Milwaukee's 1886 labor unrest, killing several people and making the site a landmark in Wisconsin labor history.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Newhall House Fire
summary: A fire destroyed Milwaukee's Newhall House hotel in January 1883. Dozens of people died, making it one of the city's deadliest nineteenth-century disasters.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Third Ward Fire
summary: A huge fire swept Milwaukee's Third Ward in October 1892, destroying hundreds of buildings and reshaping a neighborhood that later became one of the city's best-known historic districts.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Solomon Juneau Helped Build Milwaukee
summary: Fur trader Solomon Juneau established a settlement on the east side of the Milwaukee River and became Milwaukee's first mayor after rival settlements were consolidated into the city.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Milwaukee's Three Rival Settlements
summary: Before Milwaukee became one city, Juneautown, Kilbourntown and Walker's Point competed across the rivers. Their rivalry influenced the street grid and the city's early development.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Pabst Became a Brewing Empire
summary: The brewery that became Pabst grew into one of Milwaukee's defining industrial enterprises, helping make the city nationally synonymous with beer.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Schlitz Made Milwaukee Famous
summary: The Joseph Schlitz Brewing Company expanded rapidly after the Great Chicago Fire and helped establish Milwaukee as one of America's major brewing centers.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Harley-Davidson Began in Milwaukee
summary: William Harley and Arthur Davidson developed an early motorcycle in Milwaukee. Their small venture grew into one of Wisconsin's most internationally recognized manufacturers.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Milwaukee Road Connected the Nation
summary: The railroad later known as the Milwaukee Road grew from Wisconsin roots into a major transcontinental system linking the Midwest with the Pacific Northwest.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Socialist Mayors of Milwaukee
summary: Milwaukee elected a series of Socialist mayors who emphasized public works, sanitation and efficient municipal government, giving the city a distinctive place in American political history.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The New Richmond Tornado
summary: A devastating tornado struck New Richmond on June 12, 1899, killing more than fifty people and destroying much of the community.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Phillips Was Nearly Destroyed by Fire
summary: Forest fires swept northern Wisconsin in 1894 and nearly destroyed Phillips. Thousands were displaced across the affected region and more than twenty people died.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Marshfield Burned
summary: A major fire in June 1887 destroyed much of Marshfield and left roughly 1,500 residents homeless, forcing the young lumber city to rebuild.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Gogebic Iron Boom
summary: Discovery of high-grade iron ore in the Gogebic Range triggered a mining boom along Wisconsin's northern border and rapidly transformed communities such as Hurley.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Hurley Became an Iron-Range Boomtown
summary: Hurley grew rapidly during the Gogebic iron boom, becoming a rough-and-ready mining center shaped by railroads, immigrant labor and the ore industry.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The SS Meteor Carries a Strange Shipbuilding Legacy
summary: Superior preserves the SS Meteor, the last surviving whaleback ship, a distinctive rounded-hull vessel type developed for Great Lakes bulk cargo.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Old Abe the War Eagle
summary: A bald eagle named Old Abe became the mascot of the 8th Wisconsin Infantry during the Civil War and later one of Wisconsin's most famous wartime symbols.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Eau Claire Grew on Lumber
summary: At the meeting of the Eau Claire and Chippewa rivers, sawmills and logging turned Eau Claire into a major nineteenth-century lumber center.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Chippewa Falls and the Lumber Boom
summary: Chippewa Falls became a major lumber town as logs from northern forests moved down the Chippewa River to huge sawmills.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Leinenkugel Brewery
summary: Jacob Leinenkugel and John Miller founded a brewery in Chippewa Falls in 1867, creating a business that became one of the city's enduring industrial landmarks.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Black River Logging Highway
summary: The Black River served as a transportation route for logs cut in Wisconsin's northern forests, helping build communities and sawmills downstream.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: La Crosse Became a Mississippi River City
summary: La Crosse grew where river transportation, lumber and railroads met on the Mississippi, becoming one of western Wisconsin's principal commercial centers.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Pearl Street Brewing Tradition
summary: German immigration and access to transportation helped brewing become an important part of La Crosse's nineteenth-century economy and culture.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Prairie du Chien Was a Fur-Trade Crossroads
summary: Prairie du Chien developed near the confluence of the Wisconsin and Mississippi rivers as a major Indigenous gathering place and later a center of the regional fur trade.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Fort Crawford Guarded Prairie du Chien
summary: The U.S. Army established Fort Crawford at Prairie du Chien, making the community an important military post on the upper Mississippi frontier.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Villa Louis and the Dousman Estate
summary: The Dousman family's Villa Louis estate reflects the wealth created by fur trading, transportation and commerce at Prairie du Chien.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Pendarvis Preserved Cornish Wisconsin
summary: Cornish miners built stone cottages in Mineral Point. Several were later preserved as Pendarvis, documenting the region's mining and immigrant heritage.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Belmont Hosted Wisconsin's First Territorial Capitol
summary: Wisconsin Territory's first legislature met in temporary buildings at Belmont in 1836 before the territorial capital moved to Madison.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Shot Tower at Helena
summary: Workers at Helena produced lead shot by dropping molten lead through a tall shaft, using gravity to form round pellets for ammunition.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

imageAlt: Historic 1913 photograph of Taliesin near Spring Green, Wisconsin
title: Frank Lloyd Wright Built Taliesin Here
summary: Architect Frank Lloyd Wright built Taliesin near Spring Green as his home, studio and architectural laboratory in the landscape of the Wisconsin River valley.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Taliesin Murders
summary: In 1914, a servant killed seven people and set fire to part of Frank Lloyd Wright's Taliesin, one of the darkest events associated with the famous estate.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Aztalan Was a Mississippian Community
summary: Centuries before European settlement, a large Indigenous community at Aztalan built platform mounds and a fortified settlement connected to the broader Mississippian world.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Jefferson Became a Manufacturing Center
summary: Waterpower and transportation helped Jefferson develop mills and manufacturing along the Rock River during Wisconsin's nineteenth-century growth.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Watertown's Octagon House
summary: Watertown's Octagon House is an unusual eight-sided nineteenth-century home and a surviving landmark from the city's early prosperity.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Wisconsin Dairymen's Association Was Organized
summary: Wisconsin dairy leaders organized a statewide association at Watertown in 1872, helping professionalize the industry that would become central to the state's identity.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Republican Party Was Born in Ripon
summary: Opponents of the expansion of slavery met in Ripon in 1854 in a gathering traditionally associated with the founding of the Republican Party.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Fond du Lac Grew at the Foot of Lake Winnebago
summary: Fond du Lac developed at the southern end of Lake Winnebago as a transportation, agricultural and manufacturing center.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Brothertown Indian Nation Settled Near Lake Winnebago
summary: Members of the Brothertown Indian Nation established a community along the eastern shore of Lake Winnebago after relocating from the East.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Stockbridge-Munsee Built a New Home in Wisconsin
summary: The Stockbridge-Munsee Community established a homeland in Wisconsin after repeated removals from ancestral lands in the eastern United States.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Menominee Nation's Lumber Legacy
summary: The Menominee Nation developed a nationally significant tradition of sustained-yield forestry, managing tribal timberlands while maintaining long-term forest health.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Green Bay Is One of Wisconsin's Oldest European Settlements
summary: French explorers and traders established a presence at Green Bay in the seventeenth century, building on an area long central to Indigenous trade and travel.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Fort Howard Stood at Green Bay
summary: The U.S. Army established Fort Howard near the mouth of the Fox River after the War of 1812, strengthening American control of the Great Lakes-Fox-Wisconsin route.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Tank Cottage Is Older Than Wisconsin Statehood
summary: The Tank Cottage, associated with Green Bay's early fur-trade era, is among Wisconsin's oldest surviving buildings.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Hazelwood Home Tells Green Bay's Civil War Story
summary: Hazelwood was home to Morgan and Elizabeth Martin, members of a prominent Green Bay family whose lives connected territorial politics, commerce and the Civil War era.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Lambeau Field Grew From a Small-Town Football Tradition
summary: Green Bay's professional football tradition culminated in the opening of what became Lambeau Field, an unusually enduring major-league franchise in a small city.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

imageAlt: Historic depiction of the 1871 Peshtigo Fire
title: The Peshtigo Fire Cemetery
summary: A mass grave at Peshtigo contains victims of the 1871 fire whose remains could not be individually identified.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Marinette Grew From Lumber and the Menominee River
summary: Sawmills and timber moving through the Menominee River made Marinette an important lumber and manufacturing center.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Sturgeon Bay's Canal Cut Across Door County
summary: The Sturgeon Bay Ship Canal created a shorter route between Green Bay and Lake Michigan and helped establish Sturgeon Bay as a major maritime and shipbuilding center.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Door County's Cana Island Lighthouse
summary: Cana Island Lighthouse was built to guide vessels along Door County's dangerous Lake Michigan shoreline and remains one of the peninsula's best-known maritime landmarks.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Eagle Bluff Lighthouse
summary: Eagle Bluff Lighthouse guided ships through the waters of Green Bay during an era when maritime traffic was essential to Door County communities.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Death's Door Passage
summary: The strait between the Door Peninsula and Washington Island became known as Death's Door, reflecting the hazards of currents, storms and navigation in the passage.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Washington Island's Icelandic Settlement
summary: Washington Island became home to one of the oldest Icelandic communities in the United States, adding a distinctive chapter to Door County's immigrant history.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Kewaunee's Harbor Connected Farms to the Great Lakes
summary: Kewaunee's harbor linked northeastern Wisconsin farms and industries to Great Lakes shipping and later railroad-car ferry service.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Two Rivers Claims the Ice Cream Sundae
summary: Two Rivers preserves a local tradition that an ice cream sundae was first served there in 1881, one of several American communities associated with the dessert's origin.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Manitowoc Built Submarines for World War II
summary: Manitowoc Shipbuilding Company built submarines for the U.S. Navy during World War II, an extraordinary wartime effort for a Lake Michigan shipyard far from the ocean.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Sputnik Fell on Manitowoc
summary: A fragment of the Soviet Sputnik 4 spacecraft fell onto a Manitowoc street in 1962, giving the city an unexpected connection to the Space Race.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Sheboygan Became a Furniture-Manufacturing Power
summary: Sheboygan's access to lumber, transportation and skilled immigrant labor helped make furniture manufacturing a major part of the city's industrial economy.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Kohler Company Built a Plumbing Empire
summary: The Kohler Company transformed an iron and steel manufacturing business into an internationally known maker of plumbing products, shaping the village that bears its name.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Wade House Served Stagecoach Travelers
summary: The Wade House operated as a stagecoach inn on a major route between Fond du Lac and Sheboygan, preserving a glimpse of travel before railroads dominated Wisconsin.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Wisconsin's First Railroad Reached Waukesha
summary: Wisconsin's first operating railroad pushed west from Milwaukee toward Waukesha, beginning a transportation revolution that reshaped settlement and commerce.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Waukesha Became a Spring-Water Resort
summary: Waukesha's mineral springs attracted visitors who believed the water had health benefits, turning the city into a nationally known resort destination.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Old World Wisconsin Preserves Immigrant Farm Life
summary: Old World Wisconsin opened during the nation's bicentennial to preserve and interpret buildings, farms and traditions representing generations of Wisconsin immigrants.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Black Hawk War Passed Through Wisconsin
summary: The 1832 Black Hawk War moved across southern and western Wisconsin as Sauk leader Black Hawk's band attempted to escape pursuing militia and U.S. troops.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The First Wisconsin Constitution Was Rejected
summary: Wisconsin voters rejected the territory's first proposed state constitution in 1847. A second constitution was approved the following year, clearing the way for statehood.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Wisconsin Became a State
summary: Wisconsin entered the Union as the 30th state on May 29, 1848, after voters approved a new state constitution.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Madison Was Chosen as the Territorial Capital
summary: James Duane Doty promoted Madison as the new territorial capital in 1836, even though the settlement was still largely undeveloped.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Camp Randall Trained Civil War Soldiers
summary: Camp Randall served as Wisconsin's principal Civil War training camp and later became the site of the University of Wisconsin's football stadium.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Confederate Prisoners Were Held at Camp Randall
summary: After the Battle of Island Number Ten, Confederate prisoners were held at Camp Randall in Madison. Some died there and were buried in the city.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Babcock Test Changed Dairy Farming
summary: University of Wisconsin scientist Stephen Babcock developed a practical test for measuring butterfat in milk, transforming dairy production and helping Wisconsin's cheese industry grow.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Wisconsin Idea Took Shape in Madison
summary: Progressive-era leaders promoted the Wisconsin Idea: the belief that university expertise should serve people throughout the state and inform public policy.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Earth Day's Founder Came From Wisconsin
summary: Wisconsin senator and former governor Gaylord Nelson helped create the first Earth Day in 1970, turning environmental concerns into a nationwide civic movement.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Sterling Hall Was Bombed
summary: Antiwar activists bombed Sterling Hall at the University of Wisconsin in 1970. Researcher Robert Fassnacht was killed and several others were injured.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Monona Terrace Dream Took Decades
summary: Frank Lloyd Wright proposed a civic center on Madison's Lake Monona decades before a version of his design was finally built as Monona Terrace in 1997.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Ho-Chunk History Runs Through Madison's Lakes
summary: The Madison lakes region is part of the ancestral homeland of the Ho-Chunk Nation, whose history in the area long predates the creation of the city.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Effigy Mounds Once Covered the Madison Area
summary: Indigenous peoples built numerous effigy and burial mounds around Madison's lakes. Surviving examples preserve part of a much larger ceremonial landscape.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Baraboo Range Is Older Than the Rockies
summary: The quartzite ridges surrounding Baraboo are remnants of extremely ancient mountains, giving the area a geological story far older than human settlement.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Devil's Lake Became an Early State Park
summary: Devil's Lake became one of Wisconsin's earliest state parks and grew into one of the state's most visited natural destinations.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Wisconsin Dells Grew Around the River Gorge
summary: The dramatic sandstone formations of the Wisconsin River drew visitors long before modern waterparks, helping create one of the state's oldest tourism economies.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: H.H. Bennett Froze Action in Wisconsin Dells
summary: Photographer H.H. Bennett used innovative techniques to capture dramatic images of the Wisconsin Dells, helping advertise the region to tourists across the country.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Portage Grew at the Fox-Wisconsin Carrying Place
summary: At Portage, travelers could carry canoes and goods a short distance between the Fox and Wisconsin rivers, creating a strategic route between the Great Lakes and Mississippi watersheds.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Fort Winnebago Guarded the Portage
summary: The U.S. Army built Fort Winnebago near the Fox-Wisconsin portage to control a key transportation corridor during the territorial era.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Wisconsin River Powered Paper Mills
summary: Waterpower and access to timber helped Wisconsin Rapids and nearby communities become major centers of the state's paper industry.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Stevens Point Grew From a River Landing
summary: Stevens Point developed around a landing on the Wisconsin River used by lumbermen and river traffic, later growing into a regional manufacturing and education center.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Wausau Was Built on Lumber
summary: Lumbering and sawmills along the Wisconsin River fueled Wausau's early growth and created fortunes that shaped the city's later development.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Marathon County Courthouse Era
summary: Wausau's historic civic buildings reflect the prosperity that followed the lumber era and the city's rise as the commercial center of Marathon County.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Hodag Became Rhinelander's Monster
summary: A legendary creature called the Hodag became Rhinelander's enduring mascot after nineteenth-century lumberman Eugene Shepard promoted tales and displays of the supposed beast.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Logging Shaped the Northwoods
summary: Logging camps, river drives and railroads transformed northern Wisconsin as pine forests were cut to supply lumber for growing Midwestern cities.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Lumberjack Steam Train Era
summary: Railroads eventually replaced many river drives in northern logging country, hauling timber from remote forests to mills and communities.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Ashland Became an Ore and Timber Port
summary: Ashland's Lake Superior harbor handled lumber and iron ore, linking northern Wisconsin's natural resources with Great Lakes transportation.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Apostle Islands Lighthouses Guided Lake Superior Shipping
summary: A network of lighthouses around the Apostle Islands helped vessels navigate the dangerous waters and busy shipping routes of western Lake Superior.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Bayfield Grew From Fishing, Lumber and Shipping
summary: Bayfield developed as a Lake Superior port supported by commercial fishing, lumbering, shipping and later tourism.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Madeline Island Was a Major Ojibwe Center
summary: Madeline Island and the Chequamegon Bay region have long been central to Ojibwe history, culture, trade and community life in the western Great Lakes.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Treaty of La Pointe Changed Ojibwe Lands
summary: The 1854 Treaty of La Pointe established reservations in the region while Ojibwe communities retained important hunting, fishing and gathering rights in ceded territory.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Beloit Grew Around Waterpower
summary: Waterpower on the Rock River helped Beloit develop mills and factories, while Beloit College became one of Wisconsin's earliest institutions of higher education.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Janesville Became an Industrial City
summary: Janesville's location on the Rock River and later railroad connections helped it grow into a manufacturing center serving southern Wisconsin.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: General Motors Shaped Janesville
summary: Automobile manufacturing became central to Janesville's twentieth-century economy when General Motors operated a major assembly plant in the city.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Racine Became a Farm-Machinery Center
summary: Racine manufacturers produced agricultural machinery and other goods that were sold across the country, making the city an important industrial center.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Case Company Grew in Racine
summary: Jerome Increase Case built a threshing-machine business in Racine that grew into one of America's major agricultural-equipment manufacturers.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: Kenosha's Auto Industry
summary: Kenosha became a major automobile-manufacturing city through companies that evolved into Nash, American Motors and later Chrysler operations.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: The Typewriter Was Developed in Wisconsin
summary: Christopher Latham Sholes and collaborators developed an early practical typewriter in Wisconsin, helping create a machine that transformed business communication.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — State Historical Markers / Wisconsin History

title: A Tornado Gave Wabeno Its Name
summary: On June 2, 1880, a tornado tore across northern Wisconsin, flattening timber in a strip roughly half a mile to a mile wide. The blowdown became known as Waubeno—described locally as 'the coming of the winds' or 'the opening'—and the settlement that later grew here took its name from the storm-scarred landscape.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Lower North Branch Oconto River Watershed History

title: Five Sawmills Once Roared in Tiny Wabeno
summary: Wabeno became a Northwoods lumber boomtown after the railroad arrived. By 1905, five sawmills were operating here and together produced about 35 million board feet of lumber a year. The last major mill closed in 1936 as the surrounding timber economy changed.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Lower North Branch Oconto River Watershed History

title: Wabeno's Steam Logging Giant Survived
summary: The Jones Lumber Company used a Phoenix steam-powered logging hauler at Wabeno beginning in 1909. One of only about 200 such machines built, it survived the logging era and was later restored—an enormous mechanical reminder of how Northwoods crews moved timber before modern trucks.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Lower North Branch Oconto River Watershed History

title: Laona Grew Around a Lumber Company's Mill
summary: After lumberman W. D. Connor explored Forest County's hardwood stands, his company erected a sawmill at Laona around 1900. The railroad opened the forest to large-scale logging, and Laona developed as a classic company town whose economy revolved around timber.
source: U.S. Forest Service history of Nicolet National Forest

title: Camp Five Went From Logging Camp to Company Farm
summary: R. Connor Company established its fifth logging camp near Laona in the late 1890s. When nearby timber was exhausted by 1914, the company converted Camp Five into a farm that supplied meat, vegetables and work horses to its other logging camps. The site later became the Camp Five logging museum complex.
source: National Park Service — National Register listing, Camp Five Farmstead

title: Crandon's Population Exploded With the Lumber Mill
summary: When rail access finally made large-scale hardwood logging practical, Page & Landeck built a huge sawmill near Clear Lake in 1902. Crandon's population jumped from roughly 800 to more than 2,400 in only a few years as the lumber boom transformed the county seat.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Upper Wolf River and Post Lake Watershed History

title: A Kentucky Sawmill Helped Create Crandon's 'Kentuck' Community
summary: Crandon's lumber boom brought an unusual migration north. A sawmill operation was moved from Glasgow, Kentucky, and workers followed it to Forest County. Their families became part of the local community remembered as Crandon's 'Kentucks,' leaving a distinctive cultural imprint in Wisconsin's Northwoods.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Upper Wolf River and Post Lake Watershed History

title: Crandon Celebrated a New Railroad With 1,200 People and a Brass Band
summary: On December 6, 1915, about 1,200 people and a brass band greeted the first regular Wisconsin & Northern passenger train from Shawano. As the train approached along Lake Metonga, Crandon's mayor ceremonially drove the last spike, marking a major new connection for the isolated Northwoods community.
source: Crandon Area Historical Society — The Wisconsin and Northern Comes to Town

title: White Lake Was Built Almost Overnight Around a Sawmill
summary: In 1916 the Yawkey-Bissell Lumber Company began clearing land beside White Lake for a mill and an entire village. Within a few years the company town had a store, hotel, boarding house, schools, churches, two depots, a planing mill and more than one hundred homes.
source: Langlade County — White Lake Centennial History

title: A Pioneer Tried to Drain White Lake Into a Hayfield
summary: Pioneer Isaac Farrow tried to drain White Lake in 1876 so its bottom could become a hay meadow. The plan failed because the lake was much deeper than expected and was continually replenished by springs. The lake later became part of the lumber town that grew along its shore.

title: White Lake's Sawmill Cut Its Last Log
summary: On March 19, 1946, the Yawkey-Bissell Lumber Company sawed its final log at White Lake and shut down the sawmill that had created the village three decades earlier. The company's flooring operation continued, while company-owned homes and businesses began passing into private ownership.

title: Florence Boomed After Iron Was Found in the Wilderness
summary: Prospector Hiram Fisher staked an iron claim near present-day Florence in 1873 after reports that magnetic rock was interfering with timber workers' compasses. Railroad access reached the Florence mine by 1880, and a mining boom drew thousands of people into what had been a remote northern outpost.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Florence County Jail history

title: Boomtown Florence Filled With Saloons, Gambling and Dance Halls
summary: The iron rush transformed Florence almost overnight. Wisconsin Historical Society records describe scores of saloons, dance halls and brothels appearing as miners and loggers poured into town, with gambling openly taking place on the streets. The push for law and order eventually produced the imposing county jail built in 1889.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Florence County Jail history

title: Hundreds of Test Holes Scarred the Commonwealth Mine Country
summary: The iron boom around Commonwealth triggered intense prospecting. Wisconsin Historical Society surveys record hundreds of small circular test holes associated with the Commonwealth Mine complex—physical traces of the search for ore that reshaped this remote corner of Florence County.

title: Montreal Was Planned Around the Mining Company
summary: Beginning in 1907, the Montreal Mining Company built worker housing and community infrastructure beside its Gogebic Range mines. The surviving Montreal Company Location is recognized as an important example of industrial community planning and company housing in an American mining town.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Montreal Company Location Historic District

title: Montreal Mining Company Built Seven-Room Houses for Miners
summary: Among the first company houses built in Montreal were seven-room single-family homes constructed for miners in 1907. Wisconsin Historical Society records note that each cost the mining company about $740, while nearby Shaft No. 4 provided work during the Gogebic Range population boom.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Montreal mining company housing

title: The Plummer Mine Left Wisconsin's Last Iron-Mine Headframe
summary: The Plummer iron mine operated near Pence from 1904 to 1924. Its surviving steel headframe became an unusually visible remnant of the Gogebic Range mining era and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1997.
source: National Register of Historic Places — Plummer Mine Headframe

title: The Railroad Created Modern Mercer
summary: Mercer's transformation from remote forest country accelerated in 1894 when the first train arrived. Rail access brought settlers, roads, mills, stores and other businesses, laying the foundation for the community that later shifted from logging toward tourism and resorts.

title: Old Logging Camps Became Mercer Resorts
summary: As the big timber era faded around Mercer, the local economy reinvented itself. Some early resorts were little more than converted logging camps, and by the 1920s passenger trains were bringing visitors from southern Wisconsin and Chicago to fish, hunt and vacation among the Northwoods lakes.
source: Mercer Chamber of Commerce — Area History

title: Sheldon Began as a Railroad Bridge Camp
summary: Sheldon took shape in 1906 when Wisconsin Central Railway workers established a headquarters on the Jump River while building a railroad bridge and extending tracks north toward Ladysmith. Businesses soon clustered around the construction site, pulling activity away from the older nearby settlement of Fern.

title: The Flambeau Mine Opened Beside the River
summary: A copper-gold deposit discovered south of Ladysmith in 1968 eventually became the Flambeau Mine. The state approved the project in 1991, and the 35-acre open pit ultimately reached about 220 feet deep. Ore shipments ran from 1993 through 1997 before the pit was backfilled and the site reclaimed.

title: Hurley's Main Street Burned Twice in One Summer
summary: Hurley's young business district suffered two major fires in the summer of 1887. A June fire destroyed part of Silver Street, and a second blaze beginning at the Alcatraz Theater on July 9 consumed much of the remaining business district. Rebuilding replaced many wooden structures with brick and stone.
source: Wisconsin Historical Society — Silver Street, Hurley, Prior to Fires of 1887

title: Fire Nearly Erased Fifield Before Its Town Hall Was Built
summary: A major fire tore through Fifield in 1893 and destroyed the community's earlier town hall. The replacement, built the following year, became far more than a government building: its clerk's room doubled as a courtroom, marriage hall, funeral hall and even a temporary morgue while the surrounding logging country boomed.

title: The Phillips Fire Nearly Destroyed an Entire County Seat
summary: During the catastrophic forest fires of late July 1894, Phillips was almost completely destroyed. More than twenty people died as fire swept through Price County, turning one of northern Wisconsin's young lumber communities into the scene of one of the state's worst nineteenth-century fire disasters.

title: A Railroad Created Medford in the Middle of the Forest
summary: The Wisconsin Central Railroad pushed north through what became Taylor County in the 1870s. Stations such as Medford, Chelsea and Westboro opened access to immense timber stands and helped transform an isolated forest into a chain of railroad and lumber settlements.

title: Father René Menard Disappeared in the Wisconsin Wilderness
summary: Jesuit missionary René Menard vanished in 1661 while traveling through the wilderness of what is now north-central Wisconsin. His exact fate remains unknown. Later historical research mapped Indigenous trails, villages and waterways in Taylor County while attempting to reconstruct the route connected with his disappearance.

title: Rib Lake Grew Around a Sawmill
summary: Rib Lake's lumbering era began in 1881 and continued for decades. Logging camps, rail spurs and a major mill complex turned the remote Taylor County forest into an industrial lumber community whose history remains central to the village's identity.

title: Logging Camps Once Formed a Network Around Rib Lake
summary: The Rib Lake Lumber Company operated a network of numbered logging camps throughout the forests surrounding Rib Lake. Rail lines penetrated the woods to move timber and supplies, creating temporary communities whose locations traced the advance of industrial logging across northern Taylor County.

title: The Big Mill Made Hayward a Lumber Town
summary: Anthony Judson Hayward reached this area over the frozen landscape in the winter of 1878 and recognized the Namekagon River as an ideal place to collect and process logs. The enormous sawmill that followed became known as the Big Mill and helped create the city that bears his name.

title: Hayward's Big Mill Burned and Never Came Back
summary: Hayward's Big Mill burned in 1922. It was never rebuilt because the surrounding forests that had fed the operation for decades had largely been cut over. The fire marked a dramatic end to the industrial operation around which the community had grown.

title: A Logging Camp Became a Northwoods Resort
summary: A former Sawyer County logging camp was purchased by James Goodwin in 1905 and converted into a resort. Buildings reportedly used as the camp dining hall and dormitory became part of the resort, illustrating the Northwoods transition from logging frontier to vacation country.

title: Railroads Once Reached Deep Into the Forest Around Winter
summary: Logging railroads once webbed the forests around Winter and Ojibwa. Historical railroad maps preserve vanished lines and an Arpin Hardwood Lumber Company spur, reminders that tracks once penetrated areas that today appear remote and heavily wooded.

title: Defunct Logging Railroads Surrounded Exeland
summary: The countryside around Exeland was once crossed by logging railroads built to reach timber stands. Railroad historian James P. Kaysen later annotated maps of the area to preserve the locations of lines that had disappeared after the logging era ended.

title: Knapp, Stout & Co. Controlled Huge Tracts of Northwest Wisconsin
summary: The Knapp, Stout & Co. Company held vast tracts across Barron and neighboring northwestern counties. Historical maps show company lands spread among railroads, rivers, lakes and young settlements, revealing how deeply lumber corporations shaped the region's geography.

title: Barron's School Was Struck by Lightning and Burned
summary: Barron's first schoolhouse had been built only a few years earlier when lightning struck it in 1881 and the building burned. The growing community quickly replaced it as Barron developed from a frontier settlement into a regional center.

title: A Bakery Fire Became Barron's Greatest Early Disaster
summary: On October 16, 1908, a fire that began in the Gordon Bakery spread through Barron. Thirteen families lost their homes and five businesses, including the hotel, were destroyed. The city later described it as its greatest disaster.

title: A Dam Turned Barron's Yellow River Into Industrial Power
summary: A dam built across the Yellow River in 1881 supplied water power for Barron's flour and woolen mills. Within a decade three large saw and stave mills were operating, making the river an engine of the community's early industrial growth.

title: A Teenager's Turkey Eggs Helped Launch a Major Wisconsin Industry
summary: In 1922, 13-year-old Wallace Jerome placed fourteen turkey eggs under two of his parents' chicken hens in Barron. That small experiment eventually grew into one of the nation's largest integrated turkey operations and became a defining piece of Barron's agricultural history.

title: Forest Fires Left Settlers Homeless Across Barron and Polk Counties
summary: On September 29, 1898, forest fires swept through Barron and Polk counties. Contemporary state accounts estimated losses at $500,000 and reported that many settlers were left homeless, requiring relief administered through Wisconsin's military department.

title: Two Dams Failed Above Black River Falls
summary: After days of heavy rain, two dams above Black River Falls failed near dawn on October 6, 1911. The Black River surged through town, eventually washing away about 80 buildings and most of the business district. Despite the extraordinary destruction, no one was killed.

title: Houses Were Left Hanging Over the River After the 1911 Flood
summary: The 1911 Black River Falls flood did more than inundate streets: it tore away riverbanks and entire pieces of the city. Historical photographs show houses hanging above newly eroded banks, downed power lines and streets simply washed away.

title: Eighty-Five Percent of Downtown Was Swept Away
summary: By nightfall on October 6, 1911, roughly 85 percent of the Black River Falls business district had been carried downstream. Only fourteen downtown structures remained, and damage was estimated at about $2 million—an astonishing loss for the small western Wisconsin city.

title: People Have Lived Around Trempealeau Bay for About 13,000 Years
summary: Archaeological evidence around Trempealeau Bay reaches back to the end of the Ice Age. Paleoindian artifacts have been found within a few miles of present-day Perrot State Park, including an approximately 11,000-year-old spear point found inside the park.

title: Nearly 100 Ancient Mounds Once Stood Around Trempealeau Bay
summary: Woodland communities built nearly one hundred dome-shaped or conical mounds around Trempealeau Bay. About fifty survive today, along with effigy mounds and archaeological evidence of generations who used the bay's rich seasonal resources.

title: Cahokians Traveled More Than 500 Miles to Build a Community Here
summary: About a thousand years ago, people associated with Cahokia near modern St. Louis traveled more than 500 miles up the Mississippi and established a community at Trempealeau. They built flat-topped platform mounds and practiced lifeways connected to the great Mississippian city.

title: Ancient Rock Art Was Destroyed to Build Mississippi Wing Dams
summary: In 1888, Theodore H. Lewis documented human hands and other symbols carved into a sandstone ledge overlooking Trempealeau Bay. Only a few years later, the ancient petroglyphs were destroyed when the rock itself was quarried for Mississippi River wing dams.

title: Nicholas Perrot Built a Winter Fort Below These Bluffs
summary: In 1685, Ho-Chunk guides led French explorer Nicholas Perrot to the Trempealeau Bluffs. His men built a small winter fort here before moving up the Mississippi the following year, leaving one of the earliest documented French sites in this part of Wisconsin.

title: Railroad Construction Rediscovered Perrot's Old Post
summary: More than two centuries after Nicholas Perrot wintered near the Trempealeau Bluffs, ruins associated with his post were encountered during railroad construction in 1888. Antiquarians excavated and mapped the site, helping preserve the story of early French activity on the Upper Mississippi.

title: French Trade Beads and Gun Flints Were Unearthed Here
summary: From 1731 to 1736, Godefroy de Linctot commanded a French post at the Trempealeau Bluffs. Archaeologists working near the historical marker in the 1990s found French trade beads and gun flints dating to his era.

title: A Wealthy Grocer Gave Away the Land That Became Perrot State Park
summary: Winona grocer John A. Latsch believed ordinary people should have access to the Mississippi River bluffs. In 1916 he donated 1,010 acres along the Trempealeau Bluffs, creating the foundation for Perrot State Park, formally established in 1918.

title: Glacial Floods Helped Isolate Trempealeau Mountain
summary: During the Ice Age, natural dams holding enormous glacial lakes failed and catastrophic floodwaters carved through the Mississippi gorge. The floods helped isolate the 425-foot Trempealeau Mountain as the striking bluff island that still dominates the landscape.

title: The Northwoods Logging Era Gave Way to Resort Country
summary: Logging dominated Sawyer County from the 1870s into the early twentieth century. After much of the timber had been cut, former logging lands were sold for farms and resorts appeared around the county's lakes, helping create the tourism landscape associated with the Northwoods today.

title: Alma Became a Lumber Distribution Powerhouse
summary: Alma's position between the Mississippi River and steep limestone bluffs made it an unlikely industrial center, but nearby Beef Slough was ideal for catching logs floated down the Chippewa. From 1867 to 1889, roughly five billion board feet of timber were pulled from the slough by as many as 600 men working at nine river camps.

title: A Town Was Squeezed Between the Mississippi and 500-Foot Bluffs
summary: Alma was platted and settled in 1855 on an exceptionally narrow strip of land trapped between the Mississippi River and towering limestone bluffs. Its river location turned the tiny settlement into an important shipping center and later a major lumber distribution point.

title: Five Billion Board Feet of Timber Passed Through Beef Slough
summary: Beef Slough, a slow channel near the mouth of the Chippewa River, became one of the great log-handling sites of Wisconsin's lumber era. Alma companies used the protected waterway to sort and pull out timber that had been floated downriver from northern forests.

title: Women Posed With Schuetzen Rifles in Fountain City
summary: An extraordinary 1887 studio photograph from Fountain City shows Emma Protz and two other women posing with traditional schuetzen target rifles. The image preserves a striking glimpse of the German-American shooting culture that flourished in nineteenth-century Buffalo County.

title: Neillsville's Future Changed When the Railroad Finally Arrived
summary: Neillsville had grown on logging, but local leaders knew the timber boom would eventually fade. The arrival of the Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis & Omaha railroad in 1887 connected the community to larger markets and triggered new businesses serving railroad travelers.

title: Logging Built Early Neillsville
summary: The timber industry gave Neillsville its early economic foundation. By 1880, logging wealth had helped create a substantial commercial community in what had been heavily forested Clark County.

title: Wisconsin's First Territorial Legislature Met in Tiny Belmont
summary: Before Madison was the capital, Wisconsin's first territorial legislature met at Belmont from October 25 to December 9, 1836. Lawmakers huddled through the cold, passed 42 laws, created a judicial system and laid the framework for the government of the future state.

title: Wisconsin's First Capitol Arrived in Pieces by Steamboat and Wagon
summary: The building used as Wisconsin Territory's first capitol was made from prefabricated pieces shipped from Pittsburgh. They traveled down the Ohio and up the Mississippi by steamboat to Galena, then were hauled roughly 30 miles by wagon to Belmont.

title: The First Capitol Later Became a Barn
summary: After Wisconsin's territorial legislature abandoned Belmont, its first capitol building had a surprisingly ordinary second life. It was used as a home and later as a barn before Wisconsin purchased the structure in 1919 and eventually restored it as a historic site.

title: Lead Miners Gave Wisconsin Its 'Badger' Identity
summary: Thousands of miners rushed into southwestern Wisconsin during the lead boom of the 1820s and 1830s. Some lived in crude hillside shelters compared to badger holes, helping create the 'Badger' identity that Wisconsin still carries today.

title: Miners Poured Into Mineral Point Before the Land Was Open to Them
summary: Lead drew hundreds of miners and settlers into the Mineral Point area beginning in 1827 even though the land was not legally open to white settlement. Their arrival violated existing Native treaty rights and foreshadowed the rapid transformation of southwestern Wisconsin.

title: Cornish Miners Transformed Mineral Point
summary: Experienced miners from Cornwall, England, arrived in southwestern Wisconsin after treaties opened the region to American settlement. By the middle of the nineteenth century, Cornish immigrants made up roughly half of Mineral Point's population and left a lasting imprint on the city's architecture and culture.

title: Native Nations Mined Wisconsin Lead Long Before the American Rush
summary: The famous southwestern Wisconsin lead rush did not begin the region's mining history. Ho-Chunk, Meskwaki, Sauk and other Native peoples had mined accessible lead deposits for centuries before European and American miners entered the region.

title: Potosi's Brewery Began as a Small Limestone Brewing Plant
summary: Gabriel Hail established a small limestone brewery in Potosi in 1852. Over the following century the operation expanded dramatically, eventually becoming the Potosi Brewing Company and the community's largest employer.

title: Potosi Brewery Survived Prohibition by Changing What It Made
summary: When Prohibition threatened Wisconsin's local breweries, Potosi Brewing Company installed dealcoholizing equipment and kept operating. At its height the brewery produced more than 75,000 barrels annually before the historic operation finally closed in 1972.

title: Wisconsin's First Governor Built a 2,000-Acre Showplace Above the Mississippi
summary: After serving as Wisconsin's first governor, Nelson Dewey created an enormous agricultural estate near Cassville. His three-story Gothic Revival mansion overlooked orchards, vineyards, pastures and the Mississippi River from a 2,000-acre property once described as a showplace of Wisconsin.

title: Wisconsin's First Governor's Mansion Burned to Its Walls
summary: Only five years after Nelson Dewey completed his elaborate country mansion near Cassville, fire devastated the home in 1873. The blaze left little more than its brick walls standing and ended the brief life of one of early Wisconsin's grandest rural estates.

title: America's Oldest Surviving Tractor Ended Up at Stonefield
summary: Stonefield's agricultural collection includes the 1899 McCormick Auto-Mower, described by the Wisconsin Historical Society as America's oldest surviving tractor. It now sits on the former estate of Wisconsin's first governor.

title: Wisconsin's Only War of 1812 Battlefield Is in Prairie du Chien
summary: In June 1814, American troops led by William Clark built Fort Shelby at Prairie du Chien. A British force laid siege on July 17, and the Americans surrendered three days later. The battlefield survives within today's Villa Louis grounds and is Wisconsin's only War of 1812 battlefield.

title: The British Captured Prairie du Chien and Renamed Its Fort
summary: After capturing Fort Shelby during the War of 1812, British forces renamed it Fort McKay and held Prairie du Chien until May 1815. As they withdrew, they razed the fort to the ground.

title: People Lived on the Villa Louis Grounds More Than 2,000 Years Ago
summary: Long before the Dousman mansion or American forts, Indigenous peoples lived on the land now occupied by Villa Louis. For centuries, Native Nations of the upper Mississippi gathered on the island to trade before European fur traders entered the region.

title: Free Black Settlers and Enslaved People Both Lived at Early Prairie du Chien
summary: Prairie du Chien's fur-trade economy attracted free Black settlers to the upper Mississippi frontier. At the same time, U.S. officers and agents brought enslaved men and women to the area, some of whom lived at Fort Crawford and on land now included in the Villa Louis historic site.

title: A Fur Trader Became One of the Frontier's Wealthiest Men
summary: Hercules Louis Dousman built a fortune at Prairie du Chien through fur trading, lumber, land speculation and other frontier businesses. His wealth became so intertwined with regional development that a contemporary obituary suggested his biography would nearly amount to a history of Wisconsin and Minnesota.

title: A Victorian Mansion Here Had Indoor Plumbing and Steam Heat in 1871
summary: The Dousman family's new Prairie du Chien mansion was remarkably sophisticated for rural Wisconsin when completed in 1871. Designed by Milwaukee architect E. Townsend Mix, it included indoor plumbing, steam heat and other conveniences more commonly associated with wealthy urban homes.

title: Nearly 100 Racehorses Once Lived on the Villa Louis Estate
summary: H. Louis Dousman transformed the family estate into a major Standardbred horse-breeding operation in the 1880s. Facilities included space for nearly one hundred horses, a stable and carriage house, trainer's quarters and a half-mile oval racetrack.

title: The Dousman Mansion Was Built on a Native American Mound
summary: Villa Louis was constructed atop a Native American mound on Saint Feriole Island. The striking location overlooking the Mississippi connects the nineteenth-century Dousman estate with a much older Indigenous landscape.

title: The Mississippi Made Alma a Wheat Shipping Center
summary: Before lumber dominated Alma's riverfront economy, early settlers used the Mississippi to ship agricultural products. Most of the first permanent settlers were wheat farmers, and Alma quickly developed into an important wheat market.

title: Potosi's Name May Trace Back to One of the World's Great Mining Mountains
summary: Potosi's name is closely tied to mining. One historical explanation says miners arriving from Missouri brought the name with them; that name ultimately traces to Potosí, Bolivia, famous for its enormous silver mountain. Other historical explanations for the Wisconsin town's name also survive.

title: Lead Mining Helped Launch Wisconsin's Nineteenth-Century Growth
summary: Long before dairy farming defined Wisconsin's image, lead was one of the forces driving settlement. Thousands of miners entered the southwest during the 1820s and 1830s, and the industry helped lay the economic and demographic foundations of nineteenth-century Wisconsin.

title: The Dousman Family Gave Villa Louis Away During the Depression
summary: The Dousman family gave its Prairie du Chien estate to the city in 1935 for use as a house museum. The Wisconsin Historical Society initially declined an earlier opportunity to operate the property during the financial uncertainty of the Great Depression, but eventually took ownership in 1950.

title: Roche-A-Cri Was Once an Island in a Glacial Lake
summary: About 15,000 years ago, Glacial Lake Wisconsin covered much of central Wisconsin. Roche-A-Cri's sandstone mound stood above the water as a rocky island; after the lake drained, the flat-topped formation remained roughly 300 feet above today's sandy plain.

title: People Carved Rock Art at Roche-A-Cri Before A.D. 900
summary: Petroglyphs at the base of Roche-A-Cri are estimated to have been carved before A.D. 900. The abundance of rock art suggests the mound held special significance for ancient inhabitants, believed to have been ancestors of the Ho-Chunk people.

title: A Painting at Roche-A-Cri Links a Human to a Thunderbird
summary: Roche-A-Cri preserves both carved petroglyphs and painted pictographs. Among its most remarkable images is a painting interpreted as showing a connection between a human figure and a thunderbird.

title: 1851 Surveyors Found 'Hieroglyphs' on Roche-A-Cri
summary: Government surveyors visiting Roche-A-Cri in 1851 recorded what they called 'hieroglyphs of antiquated appearance' on the sandstone and inside a cave. From their appearance, the surveyors concluded that the markings must already have been centuries old.

title: The CCC Worked on Roche-A-Cri Before It Became a State Park
summary: Wisconsin's Highway Commission acquired Roche-A-Cri as a roadside area in 1937. While it controlled the property, crews from the Civilian Conservation Corps camp at Necedah carried out substantial work here before the site became a state park in 1948.

title: Ancient Bird-Track Petroglyphs Survive on the Bluffs Near Camp Douglas
summary: Several sandstone bluffs around Mill Bluff contain ancient petroglyphs shaped like bird tracks. The carvings, generally six to twelve inches long, are associated with Upper Mississippi Indigenous culture and are roughly four centuries old.
location: Mill Bluff State Park, Juneau County

title: Mill Bluff's Towers Once Rose From a Giant Glacial Lake
summary: The spectacular sandstone mesas, buttes and pinnacles around Mill Bluff once rose above the waters of extinct Glacial Lake Wisconsin. When the lake disappeared, formations including Mill Bluff, Devil's Monument and Camel's Bluff remained standing over the flat former lake bed.
location: Mill Bluff State Park, Juneau County

title: Montello Granite Went Into Ulysses S. Grant's Tomb
summary: Granite quarried in the small Marquette County city of Montello was used in the monumental tomb of President Ulysses S. Grant in New York. The historic Montello Granite Company quarry dates to 1879.

title: Montello Became One of Wisconsin's Early Granite Centers
summary: Soon after Wisconsin's first major granite quarry opened near Wausau, quarrying began around Montello. The industry grew as Wisconsin cities demanded huge quantities of granite paving blocks and curbing for their expanding streets.

title: An 1883 Map Shows a Steamboat Approaching Montello's Fox River Lock
summary: An 1883 bird's-eye map captured Montello at its industrial peak: its granite quarry, woolen mill and planing mill are labeled, while a steamboat on Buffalo Lake approaches the Fox River lock.

title: Steamboats Once Carried Green Lake Residents Before Roads Connected Them
summary: Before good roads circled Green Lake, the Norton family operated a fleet of steamboats from their dock and marina. The boats transported people around the lake from the 1880s into the twentieth century.
source: Green Lake Area Chamber of Commerce

title: Green Lake Once Had a Mail Route by Boat
summary: The Norton family did more than ferry passengers around Green Lake. Their marina held a U.S. Post Office contract for a marine mail route, and wooden boats were used to deliver mail around the lake.
source: Green Lake Area Chamber of Commerce

title: One of Wisconsin's Rarest Model Farms Was Built Near Green Lake
summary: Jessie and Victor Lawson used their wealth to develop Upper Lone Tree Farm between 1913 and 1916 as a state-of-the-art model farm. Its coordinated Dutch Colonial Revival buildings survive as one of Wisconsin's rarest intact model-farm complexes.
location: Town of Brooklyn, Green Lake County

title: Archaeologists Found 4,000-Year-Old Occupation Layers in the Kickapoo Valley
summary: Archaeologists excavating rock shelters in the Kickapoo Valley identified multiple occupation layers. One level dated to roughly 4,000 years ago, while deeper layers contained animal bones, charred remains, broken projectile points and stone flakes.

title: Highway 131 Still Follows Ancient Native Trails Along the Kickapoo
summary: The modern highway between Ontario and La Farge follows routes used by Native travelers through the Kickapoo Valley. Highway 131 crosses the twisting river eleven times in only thirteen miles.

title: Vernon County Was Originally Called Bad Axe County
summary: Before becoming Vernon County, this part of southwestern Wisconsin was known as Bad Axe County. The name was changed in 1862 to Vernon, a word chosen to evoke greenness.

title: Loggers Chopped Their Way Into the Upper Kickapoo
summary: Loggers entered the Upper Kickapoo country in the 1840s seeking enormous stands of virgin white pine. With few roads, crews literally blazed routes through the forest, cut timber in winter and moved logs toward the river for spring rafting.

title: White Pines Were So Huge the Kickapoo Bluffs Were Called 'The Pinery'
summary: The white pines along the Kickapoo bluffs were once so extensive that settlers called the region 'the pinery.' Logging crews felled and trimmed the trees, then rolled logs down cleared hillside chutes to the riverbanks for rafting downstream.

title: Kickapoo Logs Were Rafted All the Way to Mississippi River Markets
summary: Timber cut in Vernon County was piled along the Kickapoo during winter and floated out when spring water returned. Rafts continued toward Mississippi River markets including Dubuque, Galena, Davenport and Rock Island.

title: A Tiny Kickapoo Lumber Settlement Flourished for Only a Few Decades
summary: A small lumber settlement near today's Wildcat Mountain once supported a mill, post office and school. It flourished for roughly 25 to 30 years before disappearing around 1900 as the surrounding timber economy changed.

title: Ontario Was Platted Beside the Kickapoo in 1857
summary: Giles White arrived in the Upper Kickapoo in 1853 and settled near Brush Creek. Four years later he laid out the village of Ontario in a landscape where roads were little more than tracks following older Native routes.

title: Early Kickapoo Settlers Shared the Woods With Wolves, Bears and Wildcats
summary: The Upper Kickapoo was still remarkably wild when settlers arrived in the 1850s. Black bears, deer, wildcats and large timber wolves inhabited the forests, and historical accounts even describe deer getting in the way of winter logging crews.

title: Vernon County Became America's Ginseng Powerhouse
summary: Wild ginseng became a valuable cash crop in the wooded hills of Vernon County. Diggers could reportedly earn about three dollars a day collecting roots, and Wisconsin—especially Vernon County—became the country's heaviest ginseng-producing region.

title: Buckets of Wisconsin Ginseng Were Shipped for Asian Markets
summary: People once carried buckets of freshly dug ginseng roots out of Vernon County's woods for spending money. The roots were hauled to Illinois for washing and drying before entering an international trade prized for culinary and medicinal uses.

title: Wild Ginseng Became So Scarce That Farmers Started Growing It
summary: As intensive harvesting made wild ginseng scarce, Vernon County residents collected berries and created shaded ginseng gardens. The crop took about five years to mature, making disease or bad weather especially costly.

title: World War I Crippled the Kickapoo's Ginseng Trade
summary: Ginseng farming had become part of the Upper Kickapoo economy, but the market collapsed when World War I disrupted shipping. A former drying house and garden site survive within today's Wildcat Mountain State Park landscape.

title: Wildcat Mountain Was Named After Farmers Hunted a Sheep-Killing Bobcat
summary: According to local history preserved by the DNR, farmers organized a hunting party after a wildcat or bobcat killed several sheep. They tracked and killed the animal near today's main overlook, and the place became known first as Wildcat Hill and later Wildcat Mountain.
location: Wildcat Mountain State Park, Vernon County

title: A Private Land Donation Started Wildcat Mountain State Park
summary: Amos Theodore Saunders donated twenty acres in 1938 so others could experience the Upper Kickapoo's woods. Vernon County later contributed more land, and Wildcat Mountain State Park was formally established in 1948.
location: Wildcat Mountain State Park, Vernon County

title: A Rural Schoolhouse Was Moved From the Town of Liberty to Preserve It
summary: The Foreaker one-room school once served children in rural Vernon County's Town of Liberty. The schoolhouse was later preserved and furnished as a period classroom by the Vernon County Historical Society.

title: Viroqua's First Catholic Church Became a Museum
summary: Viroqua's Catholic parish dedicated its new church in 1908. After a larger church replaced it, the old building became the Vernon County Historical Museum in 1960 and later a museum devoted to local church history.

title: Glaciers Missed the Kickapoo Country
summary: The rugged hills around Wildcat Mountain belong to Wisconsin's Driftless Area, terrain bypassed by the continental glaciers that reshaped most of the state. Its steep sandstone-and-dolomite landscape preserves an older topography.

title: The Kickapoo River Travels 125 Miles to Cover Only 65 Miles of Ground
summary: The Kickapoo's extraordinary bends make it one of the defining features of the Driftless landscape. The river runs roughly 125 river miles while covering only about 65 miles of straight-line distance.

title: Roche-A-Cri's Ancient Rock Art Was Later Damaged by Vandals
summary: The ancient 'crow feet' petroglyphs at Roche-A-Cri survived for centuries but some were partially destroyed by modern vandalism. The remaining rock art is now fenced and interpreted for visitors.

title: Roche-A-Cri Also Carries Graffiti Dating Back to the 1800s
summary: Alongside its prehistoric petroglyphs and pictographs, Roche-A-Cri carries a much younger layer of human marking: carvings dating from the mid-nineteenth century through the 1950s.

title: Roche-A-Cri Was Temporarily Run by the Local Chamber of Commerce
summary: During the summers of 1982 and 1983, state budget limitations produced an unusual arrangement: the Adams County Chamber of Commerce operated Roche-A-Cri State Park because the DNR lacked an adequate operating budget.

title: French Explorers Named Roche-A-Cri for Its Giant Cleft
summary: French explorers traveling through central Wisconsin in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries called the landmark Roche-A-Cri, a name referring to the conspicuous crevice splitting the sandstone formation.

title: Montello's Quarry, Woolen Mill and Planing Mill Once Shared One Small Town
summary: A detailed 1883 view of Montello shows how much industry was packed into the small county seat. The granite quarry, woolen mill and planing mill all appear prominently around the waterways that powered and connected the community.

title: Wisconsin Granite Was Mostly Cut for City Streets, Not Monuments
summary: Although Montello granite became famous for monumental uses, Wisconsin's early granite industry overwhelmingly served city streets. Federal census figures showed more than ninety percent of state production going into paving and curbing around 1890.

title: The Upper Kickapoo Once Had More Apple Trees Than It Does Today
summary: Apple orchards were a routine part of nineteenth-century life in the Upper Kickapoo. The DNR's historical account notes that there were more apple trees in the region in 1890 than there are today, with nearly every home maintaining an orchard or at least a few trees.

title: A Ginseng Farm Once Occupied Today's Wildcat Mountain Park Office Area
summary: Before it became parkland, the farm around today's Wildcat Mountain office included a cultivated ginseng garden. Buildings on the property were used to dry the valuable roots before shipment.
location: Wildcat Mountain State Park, Vernon County

title: Wisconsin's Oldest Known Cemetery Site Lies Beside the Oconto River
summary: Copper Culture State Park preserves a prehistoric cemetery associated with the Old Copper Complex, whose people occupied the northern Midwest thousands of years ago. The DNR describes the burial ground as Wisconsin's oldest cemetery site and possibly the oldest in eastern North America.
location: Copper Culture State Park, Oconto County

title: Ancient Copper Workers Lived Along the Oconto River Thousands of Years Ago
summary: Long before European settlement, Old Copper Complex people occupied northeastern Wisconsin and worked native copper into tools and other objects. A major cemetery connected to that culture survives at today's Copper Culture State Park.
location: Copper Culture State Park, Oconto County

title: The Ancient Oconto Burials Are Connected to Menominee Ancestors
summary: Modern archaeological interpretation identifies the people buried at the Oconto Site as direct prehistoric ancestors of the Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin, connecting one of the state's oldest archaeological sites with a living Wisconsin nation.
location: Copper Culture State Park, Oconto County

title: Wisconsin's Oldest Standing Logging Camp Still Sits Where It Was Built
summary: Holt and Balcom Logging Camp No. 1 was built in 1880 and remains on its original site east of Lakewood. The Wisconsin Historical Society identifies its bunkhouse as the oldest known logging-camp building in Wisconsin still standing where it was constructed.

title: An 1880 Logging Camp Had a Cookhouse, Bunkhouse and Open Dogtrot
summary: Holt and Balcom's surviving camp building was built from round white-pine logs and divided by a twelve-foot open breezeway. One side served as the cookhouse while the other held double-deck bunks for logging crews.

title: A Northwoods Logging Camp Once Included Its Own Blacksmith Shop and Farm Fields
summary: The Holt and Balcom camp was once a small self-contained settlement in the woods. Besides its surviving cookhouse and bunkhouse, the operation included a blacksmith shop, horse barn, warehouse, truck garden, pasture and hay fields.

title: The Peshtigo Fire Obliterated Towns in Only Hours
summary: On October 8, 1871, a firestorm swept across northeastern Wisconsin and virtually destroyed Peshtigo. The Wisconsin Historical Society records more than 1,100 known deaths, with hundreds more believed killed, making it the deadliest forest fire in American history.

title: The Peshtigo Fire Burned a Swath Roughly 10 Miles Wide and 40 Miles Long
summary: The 1871 Peshtigo Fire tore through a massive corridor of northeastern Wisconsin. Historical Society accounts describe a devastated swath about ten miles wide and forty miles long, with flames spreading across multiple counties.

title: Thousands Were Left Homeless by the Peshtigo Fire
