summary: Beyond the enormous death toll, the Peshtigo Fire created a humanitarian disaster across northeastern Wisconsin. Thousands of survivors were left homeless and many more suffered serious injuries after the firestorm passed.

title: Peshtigo's Residents Had Grown Used to the Smell of Smoke Before Disaster Struck
summary: Drought had left the Peshtigo region dangerously dry for weeks before October 8, 1871. Residents had become so accustomed to smoke and ash from surrounding fires that many went to bed without realizing the catastrophe that was approaching.

title: Peshtigo Was a Lumber Powerhouse Before the Fire
summary: Immediately before the famous fire, Peshtigo was a thriving lumber town. Its harbor mill could produce roughly 150,000 feet of lumber per day, while other local mills manufactured doors, window sash and blinds.

title: The Peshtigo Fire Burned the Same Night as the Great Chicago Fire
summary: Peshtigo burned on October 8, 1871—the same night as the Great Chicago Fire. News of Chicago's disaster traveled quickly, while the catastrophe in rural northeastern Wisconsin initially received far less attention despite its far greater death toll.

title: The Peshtigo Fire Burned Across More Than a Quarter-Million Acres
summary: The fire complex associated with the Peshtigo disaster burned more than 280,000 acres across northeastern Wisconsin, affecting communities and forests in Marinette, Oconto, Shawano, Brown, Kewaunee, Door, Manitowoc and Outagamie counties.

title: Northern Wisconsin Was Marketed to Farmers After Loggers Cut the Forests
summary: As northern Wisconsin's great pine forests disappeared, state leaders expected farms to replace them. In 1895 the Legislature directed the University of Wisconsin's College of Agriculture to create a 200-page handbook encouraging settlers to establish homesteads on the cutover lands.

title: University Researchers Crossed Northern Wisconsin Photographing Life for Homesteaders
summary: To produce Wisconsin's official handbook for prospective northern settlers, University of Wisconsin staff traveled across the region in 1895 taking photographs and documenting farms, crops and the opportunities they believed existed on recently logged land.

title: Native Encampments Once Occupied Today's Council Grounds State Park
summary: The Wisconsin River site now protected as Council Grounds State Park near Merrill was once used for Native American encampments. The park's name preserves the area's long association with gatherings along the river.
location: Council Grounds State Park, Lincoln County

title: Ancient Hunters Followed Retreating Glaciers Through the Amnicon Country
summary: After the last great glacier began retreating from northern Wisconsin, nomadic hunters moved through the Amnicon River country. DNR history places people hunting mastodons in this landscape about 9,000 years ago.
location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County

title: Ancient Copper Workers Searched the Amnicon River's Rocks
summary: Old Copper Culture people occupied the western Lake Superior region for thousands of years. Around today's Amnicon Falls State Park, they searched rocky outcrops for native copper that could be worked into tools.
location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County

title: Copper Prospectors Dug Around Amnicon Falls—and Mostly Failed
summary: European-American prospectors moved into the Amnicon Falls area during the 1850s hoping its geology concealed valuable copper deposits. Most attempts failed, but traces of their searches remain visible in the park landscape.
location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County

title: A Railroad Company Once Owned the Land Around Amnicon Falls
summary: To encourage railroad construction through northern Wisconsin, the state transferred large blocks of federal land to railroad companies. The property around today's Amnicon Falls State Park became part of land granted to the Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis and Omaha Railway.
location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County

title: A Superior Pioneer Bought the Amnicon Falls in 1886
summary: James Bardon, an early Superior businessman, purchased 160 acres surrounding the Amnicon River waterfalls in 1886 after railroad-grant lands in the region were sold to raise construction money.
location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County

title: A Pond at Amnicon Falls Is Actually an Abandoned Brownstone Quarry
summary: A quiet pond beside today's Thimbleberry Nature Trail hides an industrial past: it occupies the site of a former brownstone quarry, one remnant of the extraction industries that operated around the Amnicon River.
location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County

title: Big Manitou Falls Was Nearly Destroyed by a Hydroelectric Dam
summary: In 1917 a proposed hydroelectric project threatened to submerge Big Manitou Falls. Wealthy lumberman and miner Martin Pattison quietly began purchasing hundreds of acres around the Black River to stop the development.

title: Martin Pattison Secretly Bought 660 Acres to Save a Waterfall
summary: Rather than publicly fight plans for a dam, Martin Pattison quietly bought 660 acres from multiple landowners surrounding Big Manitou Falls. He then donated the property to Wisconsin, permanently protecting the waterfall.

title: One Man's Land Donation Created Wisconsin's Sixth State Park
summary: Martin Pattison's donation of land around Big Manitou Falls led Wisconsin to establish Pattison State Park on January 20, 1920. It became the sixth park in the young Wisconsin state park system.

title: Wisconsin's Highest Waterfall Drops 165 Feet Here
summary: Big Manitou Falls plunges 165 feet through the Black River gorge at Pattison State Park. The DNR identifies it as Wisconsin's highest waterfall and the fourth-highest waterfall east of the Rocky Mountains.

title: Ancient People Quarried Quartz Beside Big Manitou Falls
summary: Native people quarried conglomerate near Big Manitou Falls to obtain fist-sized quartz stones. They carried the quartz above the falls and flaked it into knives, spear points and other tools.

title: Big Manitou Falls Was a Gathering Place Long Before It Became a Park
summary: The Big Manitou Falls area was an important landmark and gathering place for Ojibwe people. DNR history reports that a trading post was located at the falls during the nineteenth century.

title: A Surveyor Found Evidence of Ancient Copper Mining Near Little Manitou Falls
summary: Surveyor G. R. Stuntz found a broken stone hammer and work areas near Little Manitou Falls where Native people had mined and shaped copper. The evidence documented metalworking here long before nineteenth-century prospectors arrived.

title: Wisconsin's First Recorded Northwestern Copper Rush Started Below Big Manitou Falls
summary: The first recorded European-American copper exploration in northwestern Wisconsin occurred below Big Manitou Falls and along Copper Creek in 1845–47. Prospectors dug crude openings but abandoned the effort because of poor transportation, limited mining skill and disappointing results.

title: Civil War Demand Triggered 'Copper Fever' in Douglas County
summary: Rising copper demand during the Civil War revived mining dreams in Douglas County. Experienced miners arrived from Michigan, promising assay reports circulated, and what DNR history calls 'copper fever' spread across the region.

title: Old Mine Shafts Still Hide Around Pattison State Park
summary: Repeated attempts to find profitable copper left test holes, trenches, tunnels and shafts scattered around Pattison State Park. A triangular opening at the base of Big Manitou Falls and a shallow cave near Little Manitou Falls remain evidence of the failed mining rushes.

title: Martin Pattison Logged the Black River Before He Saved Its Famous Falls
summary: Decades before donating the land for Pattison State Park, Martin Pattison's company logged along the Black River. His crews operated a camp upstream of Little Manitou Falls for about three years, and remnants survive along today's Logging Camp Trail.
locationAccuracy: Black River near Pattison State Park

title: Copper Falls Was Mined During the Civil War Era
summary: Prospectors searched the Bad River gorge between Copper Falls and Brownstone Falls for copper during the early 1860s. Early maps show shafts in the canyon, likely connected to increased demand for copper during the Civil War.
location: Copper Falls State Park, Ashland County

title: Ancient Copper Miners Worked the Country Around Copper Falls
summary: Long before nineteenth-century prospectors arrived, Old Copper Culture people mined native copper veins in the region around today's Copper Falls State Park and fashioned the metal into tools and hunting equipment.
location: Copper Falls State Park, Ashland County

title: Early Northern Wisconsin Tanneries Devoured Hemlock Bark
summary: Tanneries flourished in northeastern Wisconsin because hemlock bark supplied tannins needed to process leather. The first tannery in Two Rivers opened in 1850, beginning nearly four decades of intensive local leather production.

title: A Trading Post at 'Mink River' Predated Modern Two Rivers Settlement
summary: Peter Rowley arrived from Ohio in 1835 and established a trading post near today's Point Beach State Forest to trade with Ottawa and Potawatomi people. He called the area Mink River; later surveyors named nearby Rowley Point after him.

title: Government Surveyors Renamed Mink River After Its Early Trader
summary: When government surveyors reached the Lake Michigan shore in 1841, they apparently did not know Peter Rowley's earlier name 'Mink River.' They labeled the landmark Rowley Point after him; the spelling later changed to Rawley Point.

title: Wisconsin's Early Park Builders Left Rustic Stonework Across the State
summary: Civilian Conservation Corps crews transformed Wisconsin state parks during the Depression, constructing ranger stations, cabins, retaining walls, stone stairways and other rustic features. Many of those structures remain in use today.

title: The White-Pine Boom Virtually Stripped Northern Wisconsin's Great Forests
summary: During the second half of the nineteenth century, lumber companies poured into Wisconsin's northern pinery to supply wood for rapidly growing Midwestern farms and cities. The boom eventually removed most of the region's old white-pine forest.

title: Holt and Balcom Owned About a Thousand Acres of Northwoods Timber
summary: Holt and Balcom was one of many firms that converted northeastern Wisconsin's pine forests into lumber. The company controlled roughly a thousand acres in Oconto and Marinette counties and supported crews from isolated camps in the woods.

title: A Lumber Mill Here Grew Into the World's Largest Lumber Corporation
summary: Menomonie's early economy grew around sawmills on the Red Cedar River. Knapp, Stout & Company expanded from that river industry into a vast lumber enterprise described in Dunn County planning history as the world's largest lumber corporation during the 1870s.

title: Menomonie's First Lumber Mill Was Washed Away
summary: One of the earliest lumber mills and dams at present-day Menomonie was built in 1822 near the confluence of Wilson Creek and the Red Cedar River. Flooding washed the early operation away; later mills on the site helped launch Menomonie's enormous lumber industry.

title: Seventeen Ancient Effigy Mounds Were About to Disappear Under Lake Menomin
summary: Plans to raise the Lake Menomin dam threatened to inundate 17 of 20 effigy mounds near the northwest shoreline. Archaeologists and local volunteers raced to excavate them before bulldozers arrived, finishing as construction crews reached the site.

title: Archaeologists Had Barely a Week to Save the Lake Menomin Mounds
summary: When citizens alerted the Wisconsin Historical Society that ancient mounds would be lost to a higher dam, archaeologist William Whittry assembled students and local volunteers. They had little more than a week before bulldozers were scheduled to flatten the mounds.

title: Menomonie's Lumber Mill Filled the Riverfront With Industry
summary: By the end of the nineteenth century, Knapp, Stout & Company's Menomonie complex dominated the Red Cedar riverfront. A surviving 1899 photograph shows the sprawling lumber mills, industrial buildings, bridges and smokestacks that defined the city during the timber boom.

title: Menomonie Once Roasted Thirteen Quarters of Beef for the Fourth of July
summary: Menomonie's 1899 Fourth of July celebration included an enormous public barbecue. A Wisconsin Historical Society photograph records thirteen quarters of beef being roasted and 8,000 pints of soup being served during the event.

title: Cutover Forests Turned Into Farms Across Dunn County
summary: As the lumber era declined, settlers bought the cutover lands around Dunn County and converted them into farms. By 1900 agriculture had become the county's primary industry, and many small communities evolved into dairy, mill and railroad trade centers.

title: A Lumber Magnate's Education Experiments Grew Into UW–Stout
summary: Lumber magnate James Huff Stout began funding educational enterprises in Menomonie in 1891. Those efforts expanded over time into the institution now known as the University of Wisconsin–Stout.

title: A Knapp, Stout Flour Mill Burned in 1911
summary: Knapp, Stout & Company operated more than lumber interests in western Wisconsin. A company flour mill built in 1880 survived for three decades before being destroyed by fire in 1911.

title: Knapp, Stout Owned Huge Blocks of Western Wisconsin Land
summary: Historic maps show Knapp, Stout & Company landholdings spread across Dunn and neighboring northwestern counties. The map reveals how a Menomonie-based lumber corporation controlled property far beyond its mills and shaped settlement across the region.

title: Steamboats Once Stopped at Tiny Mississippi River Communities in Pierce County
summary: During Pierce County's nineteenth-century growth, Mississippi River steamboats regularly docked at communities including Maiden Rock, Diamond Bluff, Trenton and Prescott, bringing travelers and commerce into small western Wisconsin settlements.

title: Pierce County's 'Big Woods' Were Cut Down and Turned Into Farms
summary: Much of Pierce County's heavily forested Big Woods was logged during the nineteenth century. The cleared land was then converted to farms as the county shifted away from timber and toward diversified agriculture and dairying.

title: Maiden Rock Was Once Called Pleasant Valley
summary: The township associated with today's Maiden Rock carried an earlier name: Pleasant Valley. As Pierce County's local governments took shape in the nineteenth century, Pleasant Valley became Maiden Rock.

title: Ellsworth Was Once Called Perry
summary: Before Ellsworth became the familiar Pierce County name, its township was known as Perry. Nineteenth-century county reorganization changed Perry to Ellsworth as the area's network of towns and villages solidified.

title: Pierce County Farmers Abandoned Wheat for Dairy and Livestock
summary: Falling wheat prices forced Pierce County farmers to rethink agriculture late in the nineteenth century. Many diversified their crops, raised livestock and experimented with dairying, helping establish the agricultural pattern that later defined western Wisconsin.

title: Pepin County Did Not Exist Until 1858
summary: Pepin County was created by the Wisconsin Legislature on February 25, 1858, ten years after statehood. Before that the territory had been part of Dunn County, and earlier still part of Chippewa County.

title: The Federal Government Acquired the Pepin County Area by Treaty With Dakota People
summary: The land that became Pepin County entered United States control through an 1837 treaty with Dakota peoples. The agreement preceded the rapid expansion of Euro-American settlement along this stretch of the Mississippi.

title: Laura Ingalls Wilder Was Born in Rural Pepin County
summary: Laura Ingalls Wilder, later author of the Little House books, was born in rural Pepin County in 1867. The family's Wisconsin years became the basis for 'Little House in the Big Woods,' preserving a literary portrait of nineteenth-century life in the region.

title: Wisconsin Preserves a Wood-Frame Courthouse in Pepin County
summary: The Pepin County Heritage Center in Durand preserves what the Wisconsin Historical Society's local-affiliate listing describes as Wisconsin's only remaining wood-frame courthouse.

title: The New Richmond Tornado Left a City in Ruins
summary: On June 12, 1899, a devastating tornado tore through New Richmond. Surviving photographs show widespread destruction, with homes and businesses reduced to wreckage around the railroad and Willow River.

title: Photographers Documented Rescuers Pulling Victims From New Richmond's Wreckage
summary: The aftermath of New Richmond's 1899 tornado was extensively photographed. Wisconsin Historical Society images show rescuers and crowds working among shattered buildings, bare trees and debris while searching for dead and injured residents.

title: A Book About the New Richmond Cyclone Appeared the Very Next Year
summary: The scale of New Richmond's 1899 tornado quickly entered public memory. By 1900, Mrs. A. G. Boehm had published a history of the cyclone, complete with an illustrated cover showing a tornado looming above wreckage.

title: New Richmond Was Remapped Less Than a Year After the Tornado
summary: In April 1900, less than a year after the catastrophic tornado, detailed fire-insurance maps documented New Richmond's streets and buildings as the community rebuilt from the disaster.

title: River Trade Helped Build Prescott at the Meeting of Two Great Rivers
summary: Prescott developed at the strategic confluence of the St. Croix and Mississippi rivers. In the nineteenth century, steamboat traffic connected the settlement with a broader network of river towns and commercial markets.

title: Tiny Diamond Bluff Once Had Mississippi Steamboat Traffic
summary: Diamond Bluff may be a tiny rural community today, but nineteenth-century steamboats stopped here along the Mississippi River. The landing tied Pierce County's river settlements to regional passenger and freight traffic.

title: Maiden Rock Once Received Travelers by Mississippi Steamboat
summary: Maiden Rock was among the Pierce County communities served by Mississippi River steamboats during the nineteenth century. Riverboats brought visitors and trade to a settlement squeezed between the river and western Wisconsin's steep bluffs.

title: River Falls Grew Into One of Pierce County's Cultural Centers
summary: By the later nineteenth century, River Falls had become one of Pierce County's growing cultural centers, with schools, churches, hotels, newspapers, theaters and fraternal organizations serving the surrounding farm country.

title: Plum City Became a Cultural Hub for the Surrounding Farm Country
summary: As Pierce County's rural population grew, Plum City developed into one of the county's local cultural centers. Schools, churches, hotels, newspapers and civic organizations connected nearby farms with community life.

title: Menomonie's Lumber Boom Changed the Red Cedar River Itself
summary: Knapp, Stout & Company dammed the Red Cedar River to create a holding pond for lumber, dramatically altering the local landscape. The industrial water system helped move and store timber while reshaping the shoreline around what became Lake Menomin.

title: Brickmaking Joined Lumber as an Early Dunn County Industry
summary: Although lumber dominated early Dunn County development, brickmaking was also an important employer. Both industries drew immigrants and settlers and even employed Indigenous people living in the area.

title: A 1910s Map Shows a Lumber Company's Reach Across Seven Wisconsin Counties
summary: A surviving map of Knapp, Stout & Company property covers parts of Barron, Burnett, Chippewa, Dunn, Rusk, Sawyer and Washburn counties. It provides a striking picture of the geographic reach of a lumber empire headquartered in Menomonie.

title: Menomonie's 1898 Lumber Office Already Had Telephone Technology
summary: A surviving 1898 photograph of the Knapp, Stout & Company lumber office shows employees posed around their desks and an early telephone device visible in the workplace—a glimpse of modern communications inside a nineteenth-century lumber empire.

title: A Menomonie Lumber Company Also Operated a Flour Mill
summary: Knapp, Stout & Company is remembered as a lumber giant, but its western Wisconsin interests were broader. A company flour mill built in 1880 became part of the industrial landscape before fire destroyed it in 1911.

title: Western Wisconsin River Towns Were Linked by Steamboat Before Modern Highways
summary: Before automobiles and modern highways, Mississippi and St. Croix river traffic connected western Wisconsin communities with outside markets. Pierce County history records steamboat landings at multiple small settlements along its river edge.

title: Dunn County's Farm Towns Grew Around Dairies, Mills and Railroad Stops
summary: When agriculture overtook lumber around 1900, Dunn County's smaller cities and villages increasingly served the farm economy. Dairies, agricultural mills, railroad stations and related businesses became the anchors of rural trade centers.

title: A Tornado Photograph Preserved New Richmond's Railroad Amid the Ruins
summary: One of the most striking images after the 1899 New Richmond tornado looks across widespread wreckage toward the railroad. Train cars remain visible among destroyed homes and businesses, documenting how completely the storm tore through the community.

title: Dunn County's Mound Builders Left a Landscape That Survived Into the Dam Era
summary: Dozens of ancient effigy mounds once stood near the waters that became Lake Menomin. Twenty were still known near the northwest shore when a twentieth-century dam project threatened most of them, forcing an emergency archaeological excavation.

title: The Lumber Boom Pulled Immigrants Into Dunn County
summary: Lumbering and brickmaking did more than extract natural resources: they reshaped Dunn County's population. The industries employed growing numbers of settlers and attracted new immigrants into communities along the Red Cedar watershed.

title: By 1900 Farming Had Replaced Lumber as Dunn County's Main Industry
summary: Only a generation after Knapp, Stout & Company's lumber empire reached extraordinary scale, Dunn County's economy had changed dramatically. By 1900 agriculture had become the county's primary industry.

title: Pierce County's Villages Grew Around Schools, Churches, Hotels and Theaters
summary: As Pierce County matured, settlements including Ellsworth, Prescott, Maiden Rock, River Falls and Plum City became social centers for the countryside, supporting schools, churches, hotels, theaters, newspapers and fraternal groups.

title: The New Richmond Tornado Became One of Wisconsin's Best-Photographed Early Disasters
summary: Photographers recorded the devastation of New Richmond immediately after the June 12, 1899 tornado. The surviving collection includes panoramic wreckage, rescue work, damaged churches, railroad scenes and crowds moving through the ruins.

title: Stanley's Lumber Mill Needed a Dam Before It Needed Buildings
summary: Before Stanley's huge lumber operation could take shape, a dam was built across the Wolf River to create the mill pond that later became Chapman Lake. Only then did the company build the industrial complex that would employ hundreds.

title: Hundreds Worked at Stanley's Huge Northwestern Lumber Company Mill
summary: The Northwestern Lumber Company built a major sawmill complex beside its Wolf River mill pond at Stanley. The operation employed hundreds and became one of the defining industries in the community before the mill closed in 1922.

title: Stanley's Mill Had a 'Hot Pond'
summary: Among the specialized features of Stanley's Northwestern Lumber Company complex was a hot pond used in the mill operation. The Stanley Area Historical Society preserves photographs and interpretation of the pond and the enormous mill system around it.

title: A Steam Engine Hauled 16 Loads of Logs Through the Woods Without Tracks
summary: Stanley's lumber operation used an extraordinary steam-powered hauling engine capable of pulling sixteen loads of logs through the woods without running on railroad tracks—a mechanized answer to moving enormous quantities of timber in winter.

title: Stanley's Lumber Company Built Its Own Railroad Into the Northwoods
summary: The Stanley, Merrillan & Phillips Railroad began in Stanley as part of the region's lumber economy. Its tracks eventually stretched north as far as Wallrath, carrying both logs and passengers through the forest country.

title: A Logging Railroad From Stanley Carried People as Well as Timber
summary: The Stanley, Merrillan & Phillips Railroad was more than an industrial logging line. Historical Society exhibits document that it also carried people while extending north from Stanley toward Wallrath.

title: Stanley's Lumber Workers Lived in Company Housing Called the Red Row Houses
summary: The Northwestern Lumber Company shaped daily life as well as employment in Stanley. Its industrial community included company housing remembered locally as the Red Row Houses.

title: Stanley's Lumber Empire Had Its Own Company Store
summary: Workers in Stanley's vast lumber operation lived within a company-centered industrial community that included a company store, housing and the sprawling mill complex around the Wolf River pond.

title: When Stanley's Lumber Mill Closed, the Company Gave Its 81-Acre Mill Pond to the City
summary: After the Northwestern Lumber Company closed its Stanley mill in 1922, it donated the 81-acre mill-pond property to the people of Stanley. The former industrial landscape became Chapman Lake Park.
location: Chapman Lake Park, Stanley, Chippewa County

title: Stanley's Chapman Lake Is Really an Old Lumber Mill Pond
summary: The lake at the center of Stanley's Chapman Park did not begin as a natural recreational lake. It originated when the Northwestern Lumber Company dammed the Wolf River to create a pond needed for its sawmill operation.

title: Chapman Lake Park Was Named for the Man Who Managed Stanley's Lumber Mill
summary: When Stanley's former lumber-company mill pond became public parkland, it was named Chapman Lake Park for George Chapman, the manager of the Northwestern Lumber Company mill.

title: The First Thorp Settler's Nearest Neighbor Was Ten Miles Away
summary: When James Seneca Boardman settled in the country that became Thorp and Withee in 1870, his nearest settler neighbor lived about ten miles away near Longwood. The nearest post office was at Greenwood.

title: A Thorp Pioneer Hauled Handmade Shingles 50 Miles by Ox Sled
summary: James Seneca Boardman made shaved shingles during winter, loaded them onto a sled and hauled them roughly fifty miles to Black River Falls. He sold them for supplies and made the long trip home with a yoke of cattle.

title: A Supply Trip From Early Thorp Took Nine Days by Ox Team
summary: Before railroads and developed roads reached the Thorp area, James Boardman's winter trip to Black River Falls to sell shingles and buy supplies took nine days by ox team.

title: Early Thorp Settlers Blazed Roads Through Forest With No Trail to Follow
summary: Some of Thorp's earliest settlers entered a landscape with no roads and, according to local historical accounts, not even an Indigenous trail along the routes they needed. They blazed rough roads near section lines and moved families and belongings into the forest.

title: A Diphtheria Outbreak Left Only One Student in a Thorp School District
summary: Diphtheria devastated pioneer families around Thorp in 1879. Historical accounts list eleven deaths among several families and report that, after the epidemic, Eddie Fults was the only student left in School District No. 1.

title: Two Thorp Families Each Lost Four Children to Diphtheria
summary: The 1879 diphtheria epidemic struck Thorp with extraordinary cruelty. Historical accounts say James Boardman and his wife lost four children, while C. C. Clark and his wife also lost four children during the outbreak.

title: Thorp's Railroad Bond Was Voided Because Signatures Were Collected on Sunday
summary: Thorp approved a bond connected with railroad construction, but the bond was declared invalid because many of its signatures had been obtained on a Sunday. Railroad construction nevertheless moved ahead in 1880.

title: Thorp Was First a Railroad Station Spelled 'Thorpe'
summary: When railroad track reached the community in November 1880, the railroad company named its station 'Thorpe.' That winter the local post office changed its name from North Fork to Thorp, dropping the final 'e.'

title: Before It Was Thorp, the Community Was Called North Fork
summary: The settlement that became Thorp was originally known as North Fork. Its post office officially adopted the name Thorp after the railroad arrived in 1880.

title: Thorp's Town Clerk Forged Public Orders and Fled
summary: In 1882 Thorp town clerk Charles Sheldon forged town orders worth about $250 and fled. He was later captured, convicted and sentenced to eighteen months of hard labor at Waupun.

title: Thorp's First Newspaper Lasted Only Twelve Weeks
summary: Thorp's first newspaper, The Pioneer, began publication in May 1883 but suspended operations after only twelve weeks. New owners acquired its equipment, added improved type and launched the Thorp Courier later that year.

title: Thorp Voters Rejected Becoming a Village 79 to 38
summary: Thorp's first serious attempt to incorporate as a village failed in 1886. A special election at Sargent's Hall produced 79 votes against incorporation and only 38 in favor.

title: A Thorp Dairy Shipped More Than 1.8 Million Pounds of Cheese in One Year
summary: By 1916 the Thorp Dairy Company had become a major rural processor. Historical records report that it shipped 1,832,788 pounds of cheese and 279,785 pounds of butter during that year.

title: Thorp Dairy Once Controlled Six Creameries
summary: The Thorp Dairy Company expanded beyond its home creamery beside the railroad. By 1917 it owned the village creamery plus five additional plants in surrounding communities.

title: Thorp's Library Began With Just 120 Books in a Newspaper Office
summary: Before Thorp had a dedicated library building, its public library operated from the Thorp Courier printing office with only 120 volumes. A local women's club bought many of its books and even helped convert a woodshed into a reading room.

title: A Women's Club Paid to Turn Thorp's Woodshed Into a Reading Room
summary: Thorp's Women's Union Club supported the fledgling public library by purchasing books, paying for extra library hours and financing the conversion of a back room used as a woodshed into a reading room with a table and chairs.

title: The Settlement of Hemlock Once Controlled the Head of Clark County's Log Drives
summary: The vanished settlement of Hemlock grew around a dam on the Black River that marked the upper end of major log drives. Logs accumulated in the pond until water conditions were right, then the dam was opened to send water and timber downstream.
location: Hemlock, Town of Warner, Clark County
locationAccuracy: historic Hemlock settlement, Town of Warner

title: A Lost Clark County Hamlet Once Had a Sawmill, Flour Mill, Store and Eight Houses
summary: Hemlock was once a busy little industrial settlement. Historical accounts describe a sawmill, grist mill, boarding house, store and eight houses clustered around the Black River dam before the hamlet faded away.

title: Clark County's First Telephone Line Once Ended at a Now-Vanished Hamlet
summary: The old settlement of Hemlock was important enough that Clark County's first telephone line reportedly terminated there. Today the industrial hamlet itself has largely vanished from the landscape.

title: A 1914 Flood Destroyed Hemlock's Dam and Mills
summary: A major 1914 flood ended the old industrial era at Hemlock. Floodwaters tore out the dam and left hardly a trace of the sawmill and grist mill that had once supported the settlement.

title: A Clark County Mill Worker Thought His Shaking Sawmill Might Collapse
summary: As Hemlock's old sawmill deteriorated, workers could feel the building shake when heavy logs passed through the saw. A later historical account recalled that workers wondered whether the aging structure might shake itself apart.

title: A Clark County Lumber Heir Lived in an 18-Room House With Servants
summary: Theodore Withee lived at the family's Hemlock property in an expanded eighteen-room house. Historical recollections describe servants, comfortable living and a household very different from the rough logging camps surrounding it.

title: One of Clark County's First Fords Was Famous for Its Noise
summary: Theodore Withee owned one of Clark County's early Ford automobiles. Neighbors later recalled that they could tell when he was coming simply from the sound of the car approaching.

title: A Pioneer Clark County Settlement Once Rivaled Places That Later Became Cities
summary: Longwood appears prominently on early Clark County maps from a time when later communities such as Owen, Thorp and Withee were absent or insignificant. It served as an early post office and trading station before newer railroad towns eclipsed it.

title: Hemlock's Dam Cost $21,000 in 1879
summary: The Black River dam that helped make Hemlock an important lumbering and milling settlement was built in 1879 at a reported cost of $21,000—a major investment in Clark County's nineteenth-century timber economy.

title: Early Thorp Women Sang to Scare Wolves Away
summary: A local history of Thorp recalls that before the railroad opened the forest and brought more neighbors, settlers' wives left alone during winter would sing to frighten wolves away from their homes.

title: Thorp's First Fourth of July Also Hosted Its First Recorded Marriage
summary: The settlement then known as North Fork held its first Fourth of July celebration in 1876. Local history records that the same day also brought the area's first marriage, between Louis Bruno and Nora Warner.

title: Thorp's First Town Election Drew Only 29 Votes
summary: When the Town of Thorp was organized in 1876, only 29 votes were cast at its first town meeting. Residents nevertheless levied money for roads, bridges and schools as the isolated settlement began building local government.

title: Thorp's First Frame School Cost $1,600
summary: The newly organized Town of Thorp created two school districts in 1876. School District No. 1 soon erected a frame schoolhouse at a reported cost of $1,600.

title: A $30,000 High School Rose in Tiny Thorp Before World War I
summary: As Thorp grew, its earlier school buildings became inadequate. A new high school was completed by 1912 at a reported cost of $30,000, a substantial civic investment for the small community.

title: Horicon Marsh Was Turned Into What People Thought Was the World's Largest Man-Made Lake
summary: A dam built at Horicon in 1846 to power a sawmill raised water levels about nine feet. The flooded marsh became Lake Horicon, believed at the time to be the largest man-made lake in the world.

title: People Drained Horicon Marsh to Farm It—and the Peat Caught Fire
summary: Promoters tried to turn Horicon Marsh into farmland by dredging a main drainage ditch between 1910 and 1914. The farming scheme failed, exposed peat dried out and burned, and the damaged marsh was abandoned.

title: Ditches From a Failed Century-Old Farming Scheme Are Still Visible in Horicon Marsh
summary: The attempt to drain Horicon Marsh left physical scars that remain visible today. Many straight ditches crossing the wetland are remnants of the failed early-twentieth-century plan to convert the marsh to agriculture.

title: Unregulated Market Hunting Devastated Horicon's Duck Population
summary: After Lake Horicon receded and the marsh returned, its wildlife attracted hunting clubs and commercial hunters. Decades of largely unregulated hunting devastated duck populations and helped set the stage for later conservation efforts.

title: Conservationists Brought a Destroyed Horicon Marsh Back to Life
summary: After damming, draining, farming attempts and peat fires badly damaged Horicon Marsh, conservationists began fighting for restoration in 1921. A 1927 state law authorized land purchases and a new dam to restore marsh water levels.

title: Humans Were Living Around Horicon Marsh About 12,000 Years Ago
summary: Archaeological evidence shows people occupied the Horicon basin as the marsh landscape emerged after the Ice Age. Nomadic hunters arrived as early as 12,000 years ago, followed by later Indigenous cultures whose mounds and artifacts remain around the marsh.

title: Horicon Marsh Still Has Ancient Burial Mounds Around It
summary: Generations of Indigenous people lived around the rich Horicon wetland. Burial mounds and archaeological artifacts still survive around the marsh, preserving evidence of thousands of years of occupation.

title: Dodge County Has One of the World's Greatest Concentrations of Drumlins
summary: The Green Bay lobe of the Wisconsin glacier sculpted the Horicon and Rock River basin and left elongated hills called drumlins. The DNR notes that Dodge County and the surrounding area have the highest concentration of drumlins in the world.

title: Horicon Marsh Was Once a Post-Glacial Lake
summary: As the Wisconsin glacier retreated, a natural moraine dam trapped meltwater and created Glacial Lake Horicon. The Rock River eventually cut through the barrier, lowering the lake and allowing today's enormous marsh to develop.

title: Mayville's 1946 Dam Was Dedicated to Local World War II Veterans
summary: Mayville's reinforced-concrete Rock River dam was built in 1946. A plaque on the structure dedicates it to the community's men and women who served the nation during World War II.

title: Dodge County Once Had an Iron-Mining Boom
summary: Iron ore attracted major industrial investment to southeastern Dodge County. Large-scale mining near Iron Ridge began in 1868–69, supplying ore to iron producers in Milwaukee and Chicago.

title: Iron Ridge Mines Went From Thousands to Huge Tonnages Almost Overnight
summary: Before 1868, Dodge County iron mines produced no more than about 7,500 tons annually. Large-scale investment transformed the Iron Ridge area into a far more intensive mining district serving the rapidly growing regional iron industry.

title: Mayville Was Among Wisconsin's Earliest Iron-Smelting Areas
summary: Early investors around Mayville were among the first in Wisconsin to exploit local iron ore for smelting. The industry remained relatively small until larger mining operations developed around Iron Ridge after the Civil War.

title: Mayville's Iron Industry Was Still Being Photographed in 1930
summary: A Wisconsin Historical Society image from 1930 preserves the Mayville Iron Company, evidence of the long industrial legacy that grew from Dodge County's nineteenth-century iron deposits.

title: Beaver Dam Was Drawn From the Air Before Airplanes Existed
summary: An elaborate 1879 bird's-eye map portrayed Beaver Dam from an imaginary aerial viewpoint decades before powered flight. The surviving map is now in the Wisconsin Historical Society's public-domain collection.

title: Beaver Dam's 1890 Library Became a Three-Story History Museum
summary: The former Williams Free Library was erected in 1890 in Romanesque style. It later became the Dodge County Historical Society museum, housing three floors of county artifacts and exhibits.

title: A Wisconsin Water Mill Kept Grinding Wheat Into the 1960s
summary: Barton Roller Mills was built on the Milwaukee River in 1865 and remained in operation for nearly a century. The Wisconsin Historical Society identifies it as the last mill in Wisconsin to grind wheat flour and one of the state's last mills to operate on water power.

title: A 1914 Fire Gave Barton Mill Owners an Excuse to Modernize Everything
summary: Fire destroyed much of Barton Roller Mills' equipment in 1914. Owner William Gadow responded by installing new Allis-Chalmers roller equipment for wheat and rye, modernizing a mill that would continue operating for another half-century.

title: Barton Flour Traveled by Wagon to Allenton Before Going Out by Rail
summary: Washington County farmers brought wheat to Barton Roller Mills, where flour was packed into wooden barrels. The barrels were hauled by wagon to Allenton and then transferred to railroads for shipment to larger markets.

title: West Bend Swallowed an Entire Former Village
summary: Barton developed as its own nineteenth-century village along the Milwaukee River, centered on its mill and dam. It was later annexed by West Bend, but a six-block historic district preserves dozens of buildings from the former village.

title: A Hartford Factory Started With Gasoline Engines and Switched to Cars
summary: Hartford's Kissel factory complex began with production of gasoline engines. In 1906 the company decided to build automobiles and rapidly expanded the plant, eventually creating a 15-building industrial complex.

title: Hartford Built Automobiles in a 15-Building Factory Complex
summary: The Kissel Motor Car factory expanded almost every year through 1920. Fifteen interconnected buildings formed one of Wisconsin's notable early automobile-manufacturing complexes.

title: Hartford's Car Factory Built Army Trucks During World War I
summary: During World War I, Hartford's Kissel plant manufactured Four Wheel Drive Company trucks for the U.S. Army. A surviving 1918 photograph shows workers having identification badges checked as they left the factory.

title: Women Worked at Hartford's Auto Factory During World War I
summary: Wisconsin Historical Society documentation of the Kissel war plant notes that women worked in the Hartford factory during World War I while the company produced military trucks.

title: Hartford Shipped a Fleet of 50 Taxis at Once
summary: In August 1929, the Kissel Motor Car Company lined up a fleet of fifty Bradford Cabs manufactured in Hartford and ready for shipment. The Wisconsin Historical Society preserves a photograph of the remarkable lineup.

title: A 1911 Hartford Postcard Had an Airship and Biplane Pasted Into the Sky
summary: A postcard showing Hartford's Kissel automobile plant was embellished with a dirigible and biplane literally added to the image above the factory—an early twentieth-century bit of promotional photo manipulation.

title: Washington County Used a Locally Built Kissel Truck in Its Gravel Pits
summary: A 1919 photograph shows a Kissel-built truck owned by Washington County entering a gravel pit. The image captures the Hartford automobile industry's direct role in building local roads.

title: Twenty-Eight Ancient Burial Mounds Survive at Lizard Mound
summary: Lizard Mound preserves 28 surviving conical, linear and effigy mounds, making it one of the best-preserved Native American effigy-mound sites in the nation. The site is an ancestral burial ground sacred to present-day tribal nations.

title: One Washington County Burial Mound Is Shaped Like a Lizard
summary: The burial complex known as Lizard Mound contains effigy forms interpreted as birds, panthers or water spirits, along with the distinctive mound whose shape gave the site its modern name.

title: Lizard Mound Became a State Park, a County Park, Then a State Property Again
summary: Lizard Mound entered the state park system in 1950, was managed by Washington County from 1980 to 2021, and then returned to Wisconsin DNR management—an unusual administrative journey for one of the state's most significant archaeological sites.

title: Farmers Once Cleared More Than Half of the Northern Kettle Moraine
summary: After European-American settlement, more than half of the northern Kettle Moraine was cleared and converted to farms. Much of the land later proved submarginal, helping inspire creation of a large public forest and recreation area.
location: Northern Kettle Moraine, Washington County area

title: Wisconsin Authorized the Kettle Moraine State Forest During the Depression
summary: Growing demand for public recreation and forestry led Wisconsin lawmakers in 1937 to authorize development of the Kettle Moraine forest and recreation area, reclaiming land in a landscape heavily altered by farming.

title: Cedarburg Grew Because Cedar Creek Could Power Mills
summary: Cedarburg's first permanent European-American settlers arrived in the 1840s along Cedar Creek. The creek's waterpower drove mills and helped transform the settlement into a thriving industrial community.

title: Wisconsin's Last Covered Bridge Survives Near Cedarburg
summary: The Cedarburg area is home to the historic Cedarburg Bridge, identified by the Wisconsin Historical Society as Wisconsin's last covered bridge, a surviving piece of nineteenth-century transportation history.

title: An 81-Foot Schooner Lies 130 Feet Deep Off Ozaukee County
summary: The schooner Northerner, built in 1850, lies about five miles southeast of Port Washington in 130 feet of Lake Michigan water. Much of the small lumber-era vessel remains preserved on the lakebed.
location: Lake Michigan off Grafton, Ozaukee County
locationAccuracy: Lake Michigan, southeast of Port Washington

title: A Shipwreck With Its Mast Still Standing Was Found While Searching for Another Lost Boat
summary: The wreck of the scow schooner Tennie and Laura was discovered during the 1998 search for the lost fish tug Linda E. An ROV viewed it in 1999, upright in 307 feet of water with its foremast and rigging still standing.
location: Lake Michigan off Port Washington, Ozaukee County
locationAccuracy: Lake Michigan, nine miles southeast of Port Washington

title: A 1859 Schooner Still Has Much of Its Rigging on the Bottom of Lake Michigan
summary: The schooner Island City lies in about 135 feet of water off Ozaukee County. Though partly broken up, archaeologists found much of its hull structure and rigging still present on the lakebed.
location: Lake Michigan off Mequon, Ozaukee County
locationAccuracy: Lake Michigan, southeast of Port Washington

title: A Ship Sank Off Port Washington Carrying 268 Brand-New Cars
summary: On October 31, 1929, the steamer Senator sailed through dense fog carrying 268 Nash automobiles valued at $251,000. It collided with the much larger freighter Marquette and sank off the Port Washington area with its cargo of cars.
location: Lake Michigan off Port Washington, Ozaukee County

title: The Senator Kept Running at Full Speed in Fog With Visibility Near 100 Feet
summary: Before its fatal collision, the Senator was traveling north through dense Lake Michigan fog with visibility reported as low as roughly 100 feet. Its captain continued at full speed while sounding fog signals.
location: Lake Michigan off Port Washington, Ozaukee County

title: A Lake Michigan Steamer Caught Fire Between Sheboygan and Port Washington
summary: The steamship Niagara left Sheboygan for Port Washington in September 1856 when fire erupted offshore. Its engines failed, the paddlewheels stopped and passengers and crew became trapped at opposite ends of the burning vessel.

title: The Niagara Became a Burning, Powerless Ship More Than Five Miles Offshore
summary: Within minutes of fire breaking out aboard the Niagara, its engines stopped and the center of the ship was engulfed. The vessel was left helpless more than five miles offshore, with crew and passengers separated by the flames.
location: Lake Michigan off Belgium, Ozaukee County

title: A Stagecoach Road Once Cut Through Today's Hartman Creek State Park
summary: Part of the old stagecoach road linking Oshkosh and Stevens Point still survives as a trail through Hartman Creek State Park. Many early Waupaca-area settlers likely traveled this route on the way to their homesteads.
location: Hartman Creek State Park, Waupaca County

title: Waupaca County Once Had a Giant Hop Farm
summary: George Allen's farm, on land that later became Hartman Creek State Park, grew hops for beer making. The family had the largest hops house in Waupaca County before Allen eventually switched the farm to dairying.
location: Hartman Creek State Park, Waupaca County

title: A Waupaca Hop Farm Boomed Because Eastern Hops Were Dying
summary: The Allen farm's hop operation expanded during a period when drought devastated hop production in the eastern United States. Central Wisconsin farmers stepped into the shortage and briefly made hops a significant local crop.
location: Hartman Creek State Park, Waupaca County

title: Hartman Creek State Park Started as a Fish Hatchery
summary: Wisconsin bought 309 acres here for $8,500 in 1939 and called the new property Hartman Creek State Fish Hatchery. It would not officially become a state park until decades later.
location: Hartman Creek State Park, Waupaca County

title: The State Built Allen Lake From Scratch for a Fish Hatchery
summary: After acquiring the future Hartman Creek State Park, the Conservation Department dammed the creek and created Allen Lake, naming it for early landowner George W. Allen.

title: Waupaca Bass Were Raised for Rivers That Could No Longer Support Trout
summary: Hartman Creek's hatchery raised smallmouth bass for release into Wisconsin rivers including the Kickapoo, Blue and Pecatonica, waterways that had become too degraded to support trout.
location: Hartman Creek State Park, Waupaca County

title: WPA Crews Planted the Pines That Tower Over Hartman Creek Today
summary: Works Progress Administration crews planted pine plantations at Hartman Creek in the early 1940s. Those Depression-era plantings matured into some of the tall pine stands visitors walk through today.
location: Hartman Creek State Park, Waupaca County

title: Old Logging Roads Became Hiking Trails at Hartman Creek
summary: The land around Hartman Creek still contains old logging roads once traveled by Wisconsin lumber crews. Many were later converted into hiking trails through the state park.
location: Hartman Creek State Park, Waupaca County

title: Hartman Creek Didn't Officially Become a State Park Until 1966
summary: After the fish hatchery was no longer needed, the property moved into the state parks system. Hartman Creek State Park officially opened on July 22, 1966.
location: Hartman Creek State Park, Waupaca County

title: A Waupaca Granite Quarry Shipped Stone to Chicago and Minneapolis
summary: The Waupaca Granite Company began quarrying in 1886 from a roughly 100-foot mound north of the city. Its stone was shipped well beyond Wisconsin, including to Chicago and Minneapolis.
locationAccuracy: north of Waupaca, approximate historic quarry area

title: Iola's 1860 Mill Still Has Its Historic Water-Power Machinery
summary: The J. & C. Wipf mill complex in Iola includes a flour and saw mill built in 1860. Remarkably, the historic district retains original machinery and an operating historic water-power system.

title: Iola's Old Mill Was Both a Sawmill and a Flour Mill
summary: At the south end of Iola Lake, the Wipf complex combined sawmilling and flour milling beside the Little Wolf River. The surviving district preserves buildings from a period of industrial significance stretching from 1854 to 1930.

title: A Stone Engine House From 1898 Still Stands Beside Iola's Mill
summary: Iola's historic mill district includes a rubblestone engine house built in 1898, along with the old mill office and flour-and-saw-mill buildings that preserve the community's water-powered industrial past.

title: Horse-Drawn Wagons Once Packed Both Sides of Downtown Iola
summary: A surviving Wisconsin Historical Society photograph shows downtown Iola with horse-drawn carriages and wagons lined along both sides of the street while townspeople crowd the storefronts and sidewalks.

title: Clintonville's Namesake Donated Land for the City's Schools
summary: Urial Clinton, the man whose name became Clintonville, donated land for educating the community's children. The site later held the 1918 Clintonville High School.

title: Clintonville Built a Major High School in 1918
summary: The original Clintonville High School was constructed in 1918 on land donated by city namesake Urial Clinton. Later school buildings and additions transformed the site into a multi-generation educational complex.

title: Clintonville's Old City Hall Once Had a Tower
summary: Clintonville's Romanesque Revival city hall once had a prominent tower. The tower was removed in December 1978 because of rot, while its bell was slated for display inside city hall.

title: Fremont Had to Petition the Legislature Just to Become a Town
summary: In 1867 residents petitioned the Wisconsin Legislature to create a new town called Fremont from portions of the towns of Caledonia and Weyauwega. The original three-page petition survives in the state archives.

title: New London's Fairgrounds Became a Dairy and Honey Farm
summary: Land used for the New London City Fair in the late nineteenth century was later sold to George Thern and his family. They transformed it into a farm specializing in dairy and honey production.

title: An 1881 Farmhouse Survives on New London's Old Fairgrounds
summary: The Thern Farmstead preserves an 1881 farmhouse and a collection of agricultural buildings on land once used for New London's city fair. It is one of the area's unusually intact historic farmsteads.

title: A Barn From New London's Old Fairgrounds Still Stands
summary: A wooden animal barn built in 1891 survives at the Thern Farmstead. Its history reaches back to the period when the property served as the New London Fair Grounds.

title: A 1905 Outhouse Survives on New London's Historic Fairground Farm
summary: Among the buildings preserved at New London's Thern Farmstead is a utilitarian privy dating to 1905, a small but unusually tangible survivor of everyday farm life more than a century ago.

title: A Burning Propane Train Forced Weyauwega to Evacuate
summary: On March 4, 1996, a Wisconsin Central freight train derailed in Weyauwega. Tank cars carrying propane and other hazardous materials caught fire, triggering a massive evacuation and one of Wisconsin's most memorable transportation emergencies.

title: Thirty-Four Freight Cars Derailed at Weyauwega
summary: The Weyauwega disaster began when cars 17 through 50 of an 81-car Wisconsin Central freight train derailed shortly before 6 a.m. The wreck included numerous cars carrying hazardous materials.

title: Sixteen Hazardous-Material Cars Were in the Weyauwega Derailment
summary: Sixteen derailed cars contained hazardous materials: two carried sodium hydroxide, seven liquefied petroleum gas and seven propane. The resulting fire threatened additional pressurized tank cars.

title: Flames Shot Hundreds of Feet Into the Air at Weyauwega
summary: Wisconsin State Patrol officers arriving at the Weyauwega derailment reported flames shooting hundreds of feet into the air. The threat that heated propane tanks could catastrophically explode forced responders to pull back and evacuate the community.

title: Weyauwega Faced the Threat of a Massive Propane-Tank Explosion
summary: Responders feared a boiling-liquid expanding-vapor explosion as fire heated pressurized propane and LPG tank cars. State Patrol later described the incident as one of the most dangerous transportation emergencies in U.S. history.

title: A Million Pounds of Propane Were Aboard Cars in the Weyauwega Wreck
summary: A University of Wisconsin dairy-industry account of the disaster reported that fourteen cars involved carried about one million pounds of propane, with two additional cars carrying sodium hydroxide.
source: University of Wisconsin Center for Dairy Research

title: Caustic From the Weyauwega Wreck Reached the Waupaca River
summary: About 180,000 pounds of sodium hydroxide spilled during the derailment, according to a University of Wisconsin account. The caustic material raised the pH of a ditch and then the Waupaca River.
source: University of Wisconsin Center for Dairy Research

title: Weyauwega Was Evacuated for More Than Two Weeks
summary: Residents and businesses within roughly two miles of the derailment were forced out for about two and a half weeks while crews stabilized the burning hazardous-material cars.
source: University of Wisconsin Center for Dairy Research

title: Amazingly, the Weyauwega Derailment Caused No Direct Injuries
summary: Despite burning propane cars, hazardous-material releases and a prolonged evacuation, contemporary accounts reported no direct injuries from the derailment and fire itself.
source: University of Wisconsin Center for Dairy Research

title: The 1996 Disaster Wasn't Weyauwega's First Train Derailment
summary: The internationally known 1996 hazardous-material wreck was actually one of three train derailments remembered in Weyauwega's community history.

title: A Tornado Hit Weyauwega in 1950
summary: Decades before the famous train derailment, Weyauwega was struck by a major storm and tornado in 1950, one of several disasters preserved in the city's historical record.

title: Waushara County's Towns Were Extensively Photographed Before World War I
summary: Wisconsin Historical Society collections preserve a surprisingly rich photographic record of early Waushara County, including Plainfield, Wautoma, Wild Rose, Coloma, Saxeville and other small communities before and around World War I.

title: Plainfield Had Its Own Professional Photographer in the 1890s
summary: J. W. Winkle worked as a photographer in Plainfield in 1895 and 1896, part of a network of small-town photographers who documented rural Wisconsin before snapshot cameras became commonplace.

title: Wild Rose Had a Professional Photographer by 1886
summary: Joseph Winkle was working as a photographer in Wild Rose by 1886, leaving the small Waushara County community with unusually early visual documentation of local life.

title: Waushara County Had Granite Quarries Far From Wisconsin's Famous Mining Districts
summary: Historic preservation records document quarry sites around Redgranite, Lohrville and Marion, evidence that stone extraction became part of Waushara County's rural industrial landscape.

title: Redgranite's Historic Quarry Occupied the Heart of the Village
summary: Wisconsin Historical Society records identify a historic quarry bounded by Division, Bannerman and Randolph streets in Redgranite—a reminder that the village literally grew around its stone industry.

title: The Waupaca Chain O' Lakes Begins Inside Hartman Creek State Park
summary: Marl, Pope, Manomin and Knight lakes at Hartman Creek State Park form the headwaters end of Waupaca's famous spring-fed Chain O' Lakes, tying the state park directly into one of central Wisconsin's defining lake systems.
location: Waupaca Chain O' Lakes, Waupaca County

title: A 1913 Fire-Insurance Map Preserved New London Block by Block
summary: Sanborn fire-insurance surveyors mapped New London in extraordinary detail in February 1913, recording buildings and streets on both the Waupaca and Outagamie County sides of the community.

title: Clintonville Was Already Detailed on Fire-Insurance Maps in 1892
summary: By September 1892, Sanborn mapmakers had documented Clintonville's buildings and streets for fire-insurance purposes, preserving a detailed snapshot of the small city's nineteenth-century built environment.

title: A 1917 History Preserved the Stories of Waupaca County's Tiny Communities
summary: John M. Ware's two-volume Standard History of Waupaca County documented not just Waupaca but New London, Clintonville, Weyauwega, Iola, Manawa, Marion, Scandinavia, Fremont, Embarrass, Mukwa, Northport and Ogdensburg, preserving rural community history that might otherwise have vanished.

title: An Antigo Logging Crew Was Photographed in Camp in 1886
summary: Morgan Brothers photographed an entire logging crew posed outside the buildings of D. Sulivan's camp near Antigo in 1886. The surviving image provides a rare look at a Langlade County lumber camp during the height of the timber era.

title: Antigo Loggers Posed Between Mountains of Timber
summary: A surviving historical photograph shows workers near Antigo standing between two enormous stacks of logs, visually capturing the scale of the timber harvest that transformed Langlade County.

title: Logging Railroads Reached Deep Into the Forests Around Antigo
summary: Temporary and permanent rail lines became essential to Langlade County logging, allowing crews to move workers, supplies and timber through forest country that had once depended on rivers and rough tote roads.

title: Some Northwoods Lumber Camps Were Supplied From Antigo Instead of Lincoln County
summary: An 1883 map analysis by the Tomahawk Area Historical Society notes a noteworthy cluster of lumber camps east of Lincoln County that were actually served out of Antigo, showing how far the city's logging economy reached into the Northwoods.

title: Antigo's Historic Railroad Depot Survived the Railroad Era
summary: Antigo's Classical Revival railroad depot at 522 Morse Street survives as a nationally and state-listed historic building, preserving the transportation infrastructure that helped connect the city to Wisconsin's timber and commercial networks.

title: Old Antigo Newspapers Preserved Firsthand Memories of the Logging Era
summary: As the great logging era faded, Antigo newspapers recorded memories from people who had lived through it. Wisconsin Historical Society collections preserve accounts published in 1923, 1932 and 1942 describing changing logging practices and life in the woods.

title: Tomahawk's Railroad Company Owned 51 Percent of the Company Developing the Town
summary: The Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad owned 51 percent of the Tomahawk Land and Boom Company, while the Bradleys and partners held the rest. The arrangement tightly connected Tomahawk's creation with railroad and lumber interests.

title: Tomahawk's Grand Hotel Was Named for a Railroad President
summary: When William Bradley built a modern hotel in booming Tomahawk in 1890, he named it for Alexander Mitchell, the powerful former president of the Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad.

title: Before Tomahawk Existed, Logs From Its Forests Floated South to Distant Mills
summary: Before Tomahawk's boomtown development, logging camps were already cutting Lincoln County forests. Logs were banked through winter, driven downstream during spring breakup and floated toward mills in established lumber towns farther south.

title: Tomahawk Loggers Used Railroads for Supplies Even When Their Logs Traveled by River
summary: Northwoods logging used two transportation systems at once: streams dictated where logs traveled, while workers, food and equipment could arrive by railroad and then move over tote roads to remote camps.

title: Tomahawk's First Frame House Was Built by a Lumber-Raft Veteran
summary: Ceylon C. Lincoln, who later wrote about Wisconsin lumber rafting for the Wisconsin Magazine of History, lived in Tomahawk during its boom years and is identified by the local historical society as the builder of the city's first frame house.

title: An 1887 Map Shows Tomahawk Being Laid Out Beside the Wisconsin River
summary: A surviving 1887 Tomahawk Land and Boom Company map shows numbered blocks and lots, streets, rail lines and the Wisconsin River as the new lumber town was being deliberately laid out for development.

title: Tomahawk Was Detailed on Fire-Insurance Maps by 1892
summary: Only a few years into Tomahawk's boom, Sanborn surveyors had already produced a five-sheet fire-insurance map of the community, documenting how quickly buildings and industry had filled the new town.

title: A 1901 Map Shows a Giant Lumber Yard Inside Tomahawk
summary: A 1901 Sanborn map specifically documents the Bay Mill Company's lumber yard in Tomahawk, preserving the footprint of one of the industrial operations that filled the Wisconsin River boomtown.

title: Tomahawk Had Multiple Lumber Companies Incorporated in Lincoln County
summary: Wisconsin Historical Society corporate records preserve the paper trail of Tomahawk's timber economy, including the Tomahawk Lumber Company and United States Lumber Company of Tomahawk.

title: Tomahawk's Boom Was Part of a Much Larger Lincoln County Logging Machine
summary: An 1883 map shows numerous logging camps spread across Lincoln County while the region north of Grandfather Falls was still largely undeveloped outside Ojibwe communities. Companies based in established Wisconsin lumber towns were already cutting the forest aggressively.

title: Eagle River's First Logging Camp Sent Pine Logs Floating Downriver
summary: Fur traders Joshua Fox and Helms established what local history identifies as the first logging camp in present-day Vilas County on Catfish Lake. In 1856 the camp sent its first pine logs down the river toward market.
source: Eagle River Area Chamber of Commerce

title: Eagle River's First Presidential Votes Were Cast at a Trading Post
summary: Joshua Fox operated a trading post, post office and 'wildcat bank' known as Kee Mi Con near Eagle Lake. Local history records that the area's first presidential votes were cast there in the election won by Abraham Lincoln in 1860.
source: Eagle River Area Chamber of Commerce
locationAccuracy: Eagle Lake / Kee Mi Con trading-post area

title: Eagle River's First Schoolhouse Was Also a Logging Bunkhouse at Night
summary: John O'Connor built shanties while preparing a logging operation on land that became Eagle River. One shanty served children as a school during the day and loggers as sleeping quarters at night.
source: Eagle River Area Chamber of Commerce

title: Eagle River Once Had About 28 Saloons and Muddy Plank Streets
summary: An Eagle River resident interviewed for a Wisconsin historical radio program remembered roughly 28 saloons in the lumber-boom town. Streets had plank sidewalks, while the roads could become several inches of mud in wet weather and deep dust when dry.

title: River Drivers' Spiked Boots Turned Eagle River's Sidewalks Into Splinter Traps
summary: A longtime resident recalled that Eagle River's sidewalks were made from cheap lumber. River drivers wearing corked boots chewed the planks into splinters so badly that barefoot children sometimes preferred walking in the road.

title: Eagle River's Original Railroad Depot Burned Down
summary: The original Eagle River railroad depot served the lumber and early tourism industries for decades before it burned. Its replacement, the depot that still stands today, was completed in 1923.
source: Eagle River Area Chamber of Commerce

title: Eagle River's Surviving Depot Was Finished in 1923
summary: After the earlier depot burned, Eagle River constructed a new Chicago & North Western station in 1923. The English Revival-style building survives and later became home to the Eagle River Historical Society.

title: One Eagle River Saloon Became an Ice Cream and Soft-Drink Shop
summary: The Scheribel Block housed a saloon in Eagle River's boom years. After the Zimpelmann family acquired the building, the former saloon business operated as a soft-drink and ice-cream shop during the Prohibition era.

title: Eagle River's First Electrically Lit Business Was a Saloon Building
summary: Mart Hirzel's downtown building became the first Eagle River business building documented with electric lights in 1897. The property housed a saloon and café and later became Eagle River's first brick-clad building.

title: Eagle River's Lumber Town Reinvented Itself as a Tourist Town
summary: Eagle River began as a lumbering community, but as logging declined it increasingly catered to visitors arriving first by train and later by automobile for fishing, hunting and boating. Winter recreation appeared in the 1920s and became broadly popular after the 1950s.

title: Minocqua Had 29 Saloons and Only About 15 Houses
summary: Only a few years after the railroad reached the area, Minocqua's boomtown business district reportedly contained 29 saloons, two hotels, two general stores and a small market—while the community had only about 15 homes.

title: A Minocqua Logger Went Bankrupt Because the Railroad Arrived One Winter Too Late
summary: Joseph Garland logged Minocqua island in the winter of 1886 expecting to ship his timber on the approaching railroad. Construction delays kept the line from reaching the island until the following winter, leaving Garland unable to move his logs to market and bankrupting him.

title: Thirteen Railroad Cars and Teams of Horses and Oxen Lie Under a Northwoods Lake
summary: Building the railroad into Minocqua required crossing difficult lake country. Local historical accounts describe 13 railroad sand cars, three teams of horses and six yoke of oxen lying roughly 90 feet below the water after construction mishaps.
locationAccuracy: Bearskin railroad corridor south of Minocqua

title: Minocqua's First Daily Passenger Train Took Five Hours to Go 50 Miles
summary: Daily passenger service from Merrill to Minocqua began in January 1888. Train No. 13 left Merrill at 7 a.m. and reached Minocqua at 12:05 p.m.—a little over five hours for roughly 50 miles.

title: Chicago Anglers Could Sleep on a Train and Wake Up in Minocqua
summary: The Fisherman's Special became a weekend Northwoods institution. A Friday evening train from Chicago carried nine Pullman sleepers and two coaches and reached Minocqua early Saturday morning, letting anglers sleep through the trip and wake up near the lakes.

title: World War II Shut Down Minocqua's Fisherman's Special
summary: The popular Fisherman's Special suspended service during World War II after the federal government asked railroads to curtail recreational trains and conserve fuel and materials for the war effort. The service later returned before ending in 1948.

title: Minocqua Once Had a Streamlined Train With Air Conditioning and a Tap Lounge
summary: The North Woods Hiawatha brought a striking level of luxury to Minocqua's tourist trade. Its streamlined, air-conditioned equipment included a tap lounge and dining-parlor car as railroads competed for Northwoods vacationers.

title: A 1912 Fire Wiped Out Most of Minocqua's Original Business District
summary: Minocqua's early businesses were concentrated along Front Street until a devastating 1912 fire leveled most of the district. Although some owners rebuilt, much of the town's commercial activity shifted to Oneida Street.

title: Minocqua's Logging Railroad Became the Bearskin State Trail
summary: The rail corridor south of Minocqua that once hauled timber and tourists was abandoned in 1972. Wisconsin acquired the right-of-way in 1973, and by 1977 its bridges and trestles had been adapted for the Bearskin State Trail.

title: Logging Nearly Erased the Old-Growth Forest Around Minocqua in a Generation
summary: Minocqua, Woodruff, Arbor Vitae and Hazelhurst grew amid a furious late-nineteenth-century logging boom. Within a relatively short period, much of the old-growth timber was gone, and the region began shifting from lumber extraction toward resorts and recreation.

title: Mondovi Got Its Name From Napoleon's Battlefield in Italy
summary: A Wisconsin Magazine of History account traces Mondovi's unusual name to pioneer Elihu B. Gifford. While reading about the Napoleonic wars, Gifford encountered the name Mondovi—the site of Napoleon's 1796 victory in northwestern Italy—and applied it to the Wisconsin settlement on Beef River.

title: Before It Was Mondovi, French Traders Called This the Beef River
summary: The river running through the future Mondovi area was known to early French traders as Rivière de Boeuf—literally Beef River. The English name Buffalo River later became standard.

title: A 1877 Bird's-Eye Map Captured Tiny Mondovi From an Imaginary Sky
summary: Long before aerial photography, cartographers drew a detailed bird's-eye view of Mondovi as though seen from above. The 1877 panorama survives in the Wisconsin Historical Society collection and records the young village's streets and buildings.

title: Mondovi's Rural History Museum Preserves an Entire One-Room Schoolhouse
summary: The Mondovi Area Historical Society preserves a restored one-room country schoolhouse interpreting how children in the surrounding farm country were educated before consolidated schools became standard.

title: Mondovi Preserves a Historic Farmstead, Barn and Outbuildings
summary: The Mondovi Area Historical Society's Olson Farm Museum preserves a farmhouse, barn and outbuildings as a surviving example of the agricultural life that shaped the countryside around Mondovi.

title: Mondovi's Railroad Line Was Eventually Turned Into a Trail
summary: The Omaha Railroad branch eventually linked Fairchild, Osseo, Strum, Eleva and Mondovi. The line was abandoned in 1975, and its former right-of-way later became an all-purpose recreational trail.

title: Mondovi's Largest Lake Is Only About 44 Acres
summary: Buffalo County is a landscape of rivers and trout streams rather than large inland lakes. Mirror Lake at Mondovi is the county's largest named lake, yet covers only about 44 acres.

title: A 1901 Beaux-Arts Commercial Building Still Anchors Downtown Mondovi
summary: A substantial two-story commercial building erected in 1901 survives in Mondovi with its large frieze, cornice and parapet still visible. The Wisconsin Historical Society classifies its architecture as Neoclassical/Beaux Arts.

title: Osseo Burned in a Major 1881 Fire
summary: A major fire swept through Osseo in 1881. The Trempealeau County Historical Society preserves both documentation of the disaster and imagery of downtown from before the fire, making the event a defining break in the town's early history.

title: Photographs Preserve What Downtown Osseo Looked Like Before It Burned
summary: The Trempealeau County Historical Society preserves an image of downtown Osseo dating from before the catastrophic 1881 fire, offering a rare visual record of buildings and streets that were subsequently lost.

title: The Railroad Reached Osseo in June 1887
summary: The Fairchild & Mississippi railroad project pushed west from Fairchild and reached Osseo on June 20, 1887. The connection became the beginning of the branch that later continued through Strum and Eleva toward Mondovi.

title: Osseo Was 14.21 Railroad Miles From Fairchild
summary: The new railroad measured the Fairchild-to-Osseo segment at 14.21 miles. Osseo became the first major western destination before construction continued toward Strum, Eleva and eventually Mondovi.

title: Osseo's Railroad Began as the Fairchild & Mississippi Railway
summary: The company behind Osseo's rail connection was organized in 1886 as the Fairchild & Mississippi Railway Company. Before the tracks even reached Osseo, stockholders renamed it the Sault Ste. Marie & Southwestern Railway Company.

title: A Railroad From Osseo Eventually Connected Four Small Western Wisconsin Towns
summary: After reaching Osseo in 1887, the branch pushed west to Strum, Eleva and Mondovi. The route tied a string of small agricultural communities to the larger regional rail network.

title: Osseo High School Once Advertised for Students
summary: A surviving 1914 advertisement promoted Osseo's high school to prospective students. At a time when attending high school was still optional, schools could actively compete to attract young people.

title: Osseo Had an Organized Girls' Basketball Team by 1920
summary: The Trempealeau County Historical Society preserves a photograph of Osseo's 1920 girls' basketball team, documenting organized girls' athletics in the community more than a century ago.

title: Osseo's Old High School Was Vacated in 1917
summary: Historical Society collections identify Osseo's old high school as having been vacated in 1917. A town hall was temporarily used by sixth- and seventh-grade students until it too was vacated that April.

title: Osseo's Rural Countryside Was Dotted With One-Room Schools
summary: Historical collections around Osseo document numerous rural schools—including Golden Valley, Kings Valley, South Valley, Pine Creek and Tracey Valley—showing how education was once distributed among tiny neighborhood school districts.

title: A Man Remembered as the 'Learned Hermit' Lived Near Osseo
summary: Trempealeau County historical collections preserve the story of Nicholas Bourlier, remembered locally as the 'Learned Hermit' of Kings Valley, a distinctive figure in the rural countryside near Osseo.
location: Kings Valley near Osseo, Trempealeau County

title: Osseo's Railroad to Mondovi Vanished in 1975
summary: The railroad branch that had connected Osseo westward through Strum and Eleva to Mondovi since the nineteenth century was abandoned in 1975. The old transportation corridor later found a new life as a recreational trail.

title: Lake Winnebago Holds One of the World's Largest Lake Sturgeon Populations
summary: The Winnebago System supports one of the world's largest self-sustaining populations of lake sturgeon. Wisconsin's carefully managed winter spearing tradition has made the lake one of the most unusual freshwater fisheries in North America.

title: People Spear Giant Sturgeon Through Holes Cut in Lake Winnebago's Ice
summary: Each winter, licensed spearers cut large rectangular holes through Lake Winnebago's ice and watch the water below from darkened shanties. When a lake sturgeon passes beneath the opening, the fish is taken with a long-handled spear.

title: A 212-Pound Sturgeon Came Out of the Winnebago System
summary: In 2010, a 212.2-pound female lake sturgeon was harvested from the Winnebago System. The enormous fish measured 84.2 inches long and became one of the most famous examples of the system's extraordinary sturgeon population.

title: Wisconsin's Deepest Natural Inland Lake Drops More Than 230 Feet
summary: Green Lake plunges to roughly 236 feet, making it Wisconsin's deepest natural inland lake. Its unusual depth and cold lower waters give it a very different character from most lakes in the state.

title: Lake Mendota's Famous Ice Record Goes Back to the 1850s
summary: Observers around Madison have recorded Lake Mendota's annual freezing and thawing for well over a century. The resulting ice-duration record is one of the best-known long-term lake datasets in the world and shows dramatic changes over time.
source: University of Wisconsin–Madison Center for Limnology

title: Geneva Lake Once Had Mail Delivered by a Man Jumping On and Off a Moving Boat
summary: Geneva Lake's unusual mail-boat tradition dates to 1916. Mail carriers jump from the moving boat onto lakeside piers, deliver the mail, grab outgoing letters and leap back aboard while the boat continues along the shoreline.

title: The Apostle Islands' Sea Caves Turn Into Ice Caves During the Right Winters
summary: When Lake Superior freezes safely enough, waves, spray and groundwater can transform the Apostle Islands' mainland sea caves into walls and ceilings of ice. Access is highly dependent on rapidly changing lake and ice conditions.
locationAccuracy: Lake Superior shoreline near Meyers Beach

title: A Lake Superior Storm Destroyed or Stranded Dozens of Ships in 1905
