summary: The devastating Mataafa Storm struck Lake Superior in November 1905, wrecking, grounding or damaging numerous vessels around the lake. The disaster became one of the defining storms in Great Lakes maritime history.

title: 12 Hunters and 9 Bucks at a Northwoods Deer Camp
summary: In 1915, twelve hunters gathered at a deer camp near Winter in northern Wisconsin and posed with nine bucks hanging from a traditional buck pole. A surviving photograph captures the hunters, their deer and the rustic camp, preserving a striking glimpse of Wisconsin deer-camp culture more than a century ago.

title: Six Hunters Posed With Nine Deer at an 1885 Northwoods Camp
summary: Around 1885, six Eau Claire deer hunters posed with their rifles, hunting dogs and nine deer hanging from a buck pole between rough log structures. The surviving photograph offers a remarkable glimpse of Wisconsin deer-camp culture nearly 140 years ago.
locationAccuracy: Eau Claire area; exact hunting camp location unknown

title: A 1909 Photograph Preserved a Taylor County Deer Camp
summary: In 1909, hunters gathered with their rifles in front of deer carcasses at a camp near Donald in Taylor County. The photograph preserves an early Wisconsin deer-camp scene complete with snow, tents and the hunters assembled after their hunt.
locationAccuracy: Donald area; exact hunting camp location unknown

title: A Duck Hunter Opened the 1936 Season From a Boat Near Fremont
summary: On October 10, 1936, a photographer captured a hunter standing in his boat and firing at a flock of mallards on Lake Partridge near Fremont. The image was taken on opening day of Wisconsin's duck hunting season and survives in the Wisconsin Conservation Department's historic photograph collection.
location: Lake Partridge near Fremont, Waupaca County, Wisconsin

title: Market Hunting Devastated Horicon Marsh's Duck Population
summary: Horicon Marsh once attracted enormous numbers of waterfowl—and hunters. From the 1870s into the early 1900s, unregulated market hunting devastated the marsh's duck populations. The decline became part of a much larger conservation story, as hunters and conservationists later pushed to restore and protect the marsh as waterfowl habitat.

title: Twenty-Five Elk Were Released Into Wisconsin's Northwoods
summary: After generations without a wild elk population, Wisconsin began an ambitious restoration experiment near Clam Lake. Twenty-five elk were brought to the area in February 1995, quarantined and tested, then released into the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest on May 17. The small founding herd became the beginning of Wisconsin's modern elk restoration.

title: Wisconsin Held Its First Modern Managed Elk Hunt
summary: Twenty-three years after elk were reintroduced near Clam Lake, Wisconsin's northern herd had grown enough to support a limited harvest. In October 2018, the state held its first modern managed elk hunt—a milestone that would have seemed almost impossible when just 25 animals formed the original reintroduced herd.
locationAccuracy: Northern Elk Management Zone / Clam Lake area

title: Wild Turkeys Returned to Wisconsin After Disappearing From the State
summary: Wild turkeys had disappeared from Wisconsin, but in 1976 wildlife managers began a successful restoration using wild-trapped birds from Missouri. The first birds were released in Vernon County. From that foothold in the Driftless Area, turkeys spread across Wisconsin and eventually established populations in every county.
locationAccuracy: Vernon County; represents initial restoration area

title: Wisconsin Put a Bounty on Wolves
summary: As Wisconsin's deer and other wild prey declined during the 1800s, wolves increasingly came into conflict with livestock. In 1865, the Wisconsin Legislature established a bounty on wolves. The bounty remained in place until 1957, by which time wolves had already disappeared from most of the state.
locationAccuracy: Statewide historical event; marker placed near central Wisconsin

title: Wisconsin's Wolves Returned on Their Own
summary: Wolves were considered extirpated from Wisconsin by 1960, but they were not later released here by wildlife managers. Protected wolves expanding naturally from Minnesota crossed back into northwestern Wisconsin, and in 1978 the state's first confirmed returning breeding pack was documented in Douglas County.
locationAccuracy: Douglas County; represents location of first confirmed breeding pack

title: Wisconsin's Black Bears Came Back From a Historic Decline
summary: Black bears once lived throughout Wisconsin, but habitat loss and unregulated market hunting caused their numbers and range to collapse. By 1950, bears were largely confined to the northern third of the state. Increased protection, changing attitudes and regulated management helped the population recover and expand again.
locationAccuracy: Northern Wisconsin; represents historic core bear range

title: Wisconsin Built a Massive Game Farm to Raise Wildlife
summary: Wisconsin moved its experimental game and fur farm to Poynette in 1934. Working with the WPA and Civilian Conservation Corps, the Conservation Department built a major propagation center that raised pheasants, grouse, quail, turkeys, prairie chickens, waterfowl and even furbearers. A hatchery capable of incubating 150,000 game-bird eggs was completed in 1938.

title: Wisconsin Has Released Millions of Pheasants
summary: Wisconsin began state pheasant stocking in 1928 as the ring-necked pheasant was becoming an increasingly popular game bird. Over the decades, the State Game Farm and cooperative programs produced and released more than 12 million pheasants, creating one of Wisconsin's longest-running wildlife propagation programs.

title: Sharp-Tailed Grouse Once Lived Across Wisconsin
summary: Sharp-tailed grouse were historically found across Wisconsin, thriving in open pine and oak barrens and savanna. Beginning in the early 1900s, habitat loss and fragmentation drove a long decline. Wisconsin began focused management in the late 1940s and early 1950s, and today most remaining birds are concentrated in the northwest.
locationAccuracy: Northwestern Wisconsin; representative of remaining barrens habitat

title: Hunters Hauled Their Deer Out of the Oconto County Woods
summary: In 1910, a photographer captured a group of hunters bringing a deer out of the woods in Oconto County. Frank Langeois, son of Joseph Langeois Jr., stands in the center of the surviving photograph. It preserves a simple but vivid scene from Northeast Wisconsin deer hunting more than a century ago.
locationAccuracy: Oconto County; exact hunting location unknown

title: Four Deer Were Hung From the Trees Along a Cassville Sidewalk
summary: Around 1910, hunters in Cassville posed with their guns while four harvested deer hung from trees beside a sidewalk. A small child stood nearby as photographer Frank Feiker captured the scene—a striking glimpse of how publicly the annual deer harvest was once displayed in Wisconsin communities.

title: Two Bucks Were Displayed on a Downtown Burlington Sidewalk
summary: In 1900, two harvested bucks were laid out on the wooden sidewalk in front of the Schwaller building on Pine Street in Burlington. Frank A. Schwaller and his son were among the men photographed with the deer, showing just how closely Wisconsin's hunting culture once intersected with everyday downtown life.
location: Pine Street, Burlington, Racine County, Wisconsin
locationAccuracy: Pine Street, Burlington; marker represents downtown

title: Five Hunters Posed Beside Their Deer at a Taylor County Camp
summary: In March 1905, five hunters gathered for a photograph at a deer camp near Donald in Taylor County. Deer carcasses hung from a log pole beside the camp, preserving another remarkable view of the Northwoods hunting-camp tradition during the early 20th century.
locationAccuracy: Donald area; exact camp location unknown

title: Hunters Once Carried Deer Out of the Woods on a Pole
summary: A surviving photograph from the Donald area shows three hunters walking through the woods with their rifles while two of the men carry a harvested deer suspended from a pole across their shoulders. Before ATVs and modern hunting equipment, getting a deer out of the Northwoods could itself be a serious piece of work.
locationAccuracy: Donald area; exact hunting location unknown

title: Three Deer Rode Into Madison Strapped to a Station Wagon
summary: In November 1959, Danny Sands and Dick Goldfield were photographed beside a wood-sided station wagon carrying three harvested deer. Two were strapped across the hood and another rode on the roof with its antlers prominently displayed—a scene from an era when returning from deer camp could make the vehicle itself part of the trophy display.

title: A 1949 Deer Hunt Was Photographed on Madeline Island
summary: In 1949, three hunters were photographed in a clearing on Madeline Island with two harvested deer lying in front of them. One man held a rifle and another a shotgun, preserving a glimpse of deer hunting on Wisconsin's largest Lake Superior island.
locationAccuracy: Madeline Island; exact hunting location unknown

title: Five Chippewa Falls Hunters Came Back With Seven Deer
summary: In 1947, five Chippewa Falls deer hunters posed with their rifles in front of a buck pole holding seven harvested deer. A small animal, possibly a rabbit, also hung from the pole beside a log building—an unmistakable snapshot of postwar Wisconsin deer-camp culture.
locationAccuracy: Chippewa Falls area; exact hunting camp location unknown

title: Three Deer, a Car and a Very Curious Cat
summary: Around 1948, four men and a woman posed around a car near New Miner with three harvested deer stretched across its hood. But the strangest detail may be at the front of the car: a cat stood with its paws against the vehicle, staring up at the deer. John E. Limbach's photograph preserved the wonderfully odd scene.
locationAccuracy: New Miner area; photograph identified as George Sterbens Farm

title: Eight Hunters Displayed Six Deer at Wisconsin's Slovenian Settlement
summary: In 1912, eight hunters gathered for a photograph at the Slovenian settlement at Willard in Clark County. Six harvested deer hung behind the group while the hunters posed with their guns, preserving a glimpse of how immigrant communities carried Wisconsin's growing deer-camp tradition into the Northwoods.

title: Hunters Once Brought Their Deer Home by Railroad
summary: Before pickups and ATVs became part of deer camp, the railroad was one way Wisconsin hunters reached the Northwoods and brought their harvest home. A surviving photograph from Harshaw shows a group of hunters standing with their guns and harvested deer on the railroad platform.

title: The Schooner Lucerne Sank With Iron Ore Near Long Island
summary: The 195-foot schooner Lucerne sank near Long Island in 1886. Its upright hull and iron-ore cargo remain visible on the lakebed.

title: Fire Sent the Schooner Barge Noquebay to the Bottom
summary: The 205-foot schooner barge Noquebay burned and sank at Julian Bay. Sections of its wooden hull, boiler and wheel survive underwater.

title: The Sevona Broke Apart on Sand Island Shoals
summary: The bulk freighter Sevona struck a shoal during a September 1905 storm. Seven crew members drowned and pieces of its steel hull remain on the bottom.

title: The Pretoria Foundered Near Outer Island
summary: The large schooner barge Pretoria sank during the same September 1905 storm that wrecked the Sevona. Five people died.
location: Northeast of Outer Island, Lake Superior

title: Michigan Island Lit Its First Lighthouse in 1857
summary: Michigan Island’s first lighthouse entered service in 1857, was abandoned the following year and was relit in 1869.

title: The Old La Pointe Lighthouse Guided Ships From Long Island
summary: Built in 1858, the Old La Pointe Lighthouse on Long Island served Lake Superior shipping until 1897. Its foundation ruins remain.

title: Raspberry Island Lighthouse First Shone in 1863
summary: Raspberry Island Lighthouse began operating in 1863. Its building was enlarged in 1906 and the light was automated in 1947.

title: Outer Island Lighthouse Began Watching Lake Superior
summary: Outer Island Lighthouse was built in 1874 to help mariners navigate the Apostle Islands and was automated in 1961.

title: Sand Island Lighthouse Was Built in 1881
summary: Sand Island Lighthouse was built in 1881. Its light was automated in 1921, and the beacon returned to the historic building in 1985.

title: Devils Island Lighthouse Entered Service in 1901
summary: A temporary tower appeared in 1891; the permanent Devils Island tower was built in 1898 and entered service in 1901.

title: Basswood Island Still Has Submerged Quarry Docks
summary: Submerged dock cribs off Basswood Island are remnants of sandstone quarry operations active in the 1890s.

title: Stockton Island Has a Historic Dock Beneath the Water
summary: Underwater dock cribs near Stockton Island’s southwest shore preserve evidence of historic Apostle Islands quarry shipping.

title: Hermit Island Hides an Old Quarry Dock Underwater
summary: Submerged dock cribs off Hermit Island mark the maritime infrastructure of the islands’ sandstone quarry era.

title: Devils Island Waves Carved Sandstone Sea Caves
summary: Waves, freezing and thawing carved arches and chambers into the thinly bedded sandstone at Devils Island.

title: Sand Island Has Sea Caves at Swallow Point
summary: Swallow Point’s sandstone shoreline holds sea caves shaped by Lake Superior waves and seasonal freeze-thaw cycles.

title: Mainland Sea Caves Reveal Ancient Lake Superior Sandstone
summary: The mainland sea caves near Mawikwe Bay expose sandstone sculpted into arches, pillars and chambers by the lake.

title: Lake Superior Has a 400-Mile Wisconsin Water Trail
summary: Wisconsin’s Lake Superior Water Trail spans more than 400 miles of shoreline, linking paddling access, coastal communities and wild shoreline.

title: Wisconsin’s Lake Michigan Water Trail Runs 523 Miles
summary: Wisconsin’s designated Lake Michigan Water Trail follows 523 miles of coastline and connects access points across eleven lakeside counties.

title: The St. Louis River Estuary Opens Wisconsin’s Superior Shore
summary: The St. Louis River estuary forms the western end of Wisconsin’s Lake Superior Water Trail, combining extensive wetlands with the busy Duluth–Superior harbor.

title: The Kakagon and Bad River Sloughs Form a Vast Coastal Wetland
summary: The Kakagon–Bad River Sloughs are a major Lake Superior coastal wetland within the Bad River Reservation, along Wisconsin’s northern water trail.

title: A Sand Island Lighthouse Keeper Rescued the Prussia Crew
summary: In 1885, Sand Island lighthouse keeper Charles Lederle spotted the burning steamer Prussia, rowed several miles into Lake Superior and rescued its entire crew.
source: National Park Service — Sand Island Light

title: The Pretoria Survivors Were Pulled Ashore by a Lighthouse Keeper
summary: After the schooner-barge Pretoria sank in a September storm, Outer Island lighthouse keeper John Irvine rescued five surviving crew members from the surf. Five others died.
source: National Park Service — People and Places: A Human History of the Apostle Islands

title: Bark Bay Slough Hides a Lagoon Behind a Sand Spit
summary: A roughly two-mile sand spit separates Lake Superior from Bark Bay Slough’s lagoon, coastal fen and bog, creating habitat for rare plants.

title: The Bad River Sloughs Hold Great Lakes Wild Rice Beds
summary: The Kakagon and Bad River Sloughs contain the largest natural wild rice bed on the Great Lakes and are recognized as wetlands of international importance.

title: Chequamegon Bay Supports a Diverse Cold-Water Fishery
summary: The waters around Chequamegon Bay support seasonal fishing for walleye, northern pike, smallmouth bass, perch, trout and salmon.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Fishing Calendar for Lake Superior

title: A Sandstone Island Above the Central Sands
summary: Roche-A-Cri Mound once rose as a rocky island above Glacial Lake Wisconsin. Its flat-topped sandstone ridge now stands roughly 300 feet above the surrounding sand plain.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Roche-A-Cri State Park — Nature

title: Ancient Images at the Foot of Roche-A-Cri
summary: Petroglyphs and pictographs made by Native Americans survive at the base of Roche-A-Cri Mound, where a viewing platform helps protect the rock art.

title: A Cool Northern Forest Hides in a Southern Gorge
summary: Parfrey's Glen stays cool and moist beneath mossy sandstone walls, allowing plants more typical of northern Wisconsin to grow in Sauk County.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Parfrey's Glen State Natural Area

title: Wisconsin Protected This Gorge First
summary: Parfrey's Glen became Wisconsin's first designated State Natural Area in 1952, protecting a deep sandstone gorge and its unusual plant communities.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Parfrey's Glen State Natural Area

title: The Sandstone Arch the Glaciers Missed
summary: Natural Bridge State Park protects a sandstone arch formed by erosion in a part of Wisconsin that escaped the last glaciation. The opening is about 25 feet high and 35 feet wide.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Natural Bridge State Park

title: An Ancient Campsite Beneath a Natural Arch
summary: Excavations at the rock shelter near Natural Bridge found evidence of human use dating back roughly 10,000 to 12,000 years. The shelter may have served as a seasonal hunting camp.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Natural Bridge State Park — History

title: The Earthquake Fault Beneath Amnicon Falls
summary: Amnicon Falls exposes the Douglas Fault, an ancient break in the bedrock that records major geological movement about half a billion years ago.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Amnicon Falls State Park — Geology

title: Ancient Lava Still Shows at the Upper Falls
summary: Dark basalt at Amnicon Falls formed from lava that flowed across this region roughly a billion years ago; the lower falls cross younger sandstone.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Amnicon Falls State Park — Geology

title: A Quarry Became a Wildlife Pond
summary: The Thimbleberry Nature Trail at Amnicon Falls leads to a pond that was once a brownstone quarry, a reminder of the area’s stone industry.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Amnicon Falls State Park — Hiking

title: Wisconsin’s Tallest Waterfall Drops 165 Feet
summary: Big Manitou Falls plunges 165 feet within Pattison State Park, making it the tallest waterfall in Wisconsin.

title: The Smaller Manitou Falls Has Two Drops
summary: Pattison State Park also protects Twin Little Manitou Falls, a 31-foot waterfall distinct from the park’s much taller Big Manitou Falls.

title: A Blufftop Campsite 500 Feet Above Two Rivers
summary: Wyalusing State Park has blufftop camping and overlooks about 500 feet above the meeting of the Wisconsin and Mississippi rivers.

title: Ancient Burial Mounds Survive at Wyalusing
summary: Wyalusing State Park preserves Native American burial mounds alongside its bluff trails and overlooks above the Mississippi River.

title: A Prairie Survives on Brady’s Bluff
summary: Brady’s Bluff Prairie is a designated State Natural Area within Perrot State Park, where prairie habitat persists among steep wooded slopes above the Mississippi.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Perrot State Park — Nature

title: A Mountain Rises Beside Trempealeau Bay
summary: Trempealeau Mountain is a designated State Natural Area within Perrot State Park, surrounded by wetlands, blufftop forests and Mississippi River habitat.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Perrot State Park — Nature

title: More Than 200 Bird Species Around One Park
summary: The mix of wetlands, prairies and wooded bluffs at Perrot State Park makes it possible to record more than 200 bird species over a year.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Perrot State Park — Nature

title: A Century-Old Forest Beside the Bad River
summary: A sugar maple–hemlock forest along the steep slopes of the Bad River in Copper Falls State Natural Area has remained undisturbed since at least 1916.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Copper Falls State Natural Area

title: Two Old River Bends Shelter Northern Forest
summary: Two oxbows on the low terraces of the Bad River at Copper Falls support a diverse forest with white pine, maple, ash, hemlock and cedar.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Copper Falls State Natural Area

title: A 1,200-Mile Trail Traces the Ice Age
summary: The Ice Age National Scenic Trail follows the landscape left by Wisconsin’s last great glacier, crossing prairies, forests and glacial landforms across the state.
source: National Park Service — Ice Age Trail
location: Wisconsin — representative point near Cross Plains

title: The Ice Age Trail Starts at a Lake Michigan Shore
summary: Potawatomi State Park is the eastern end of the Ice Age National Scenic Trail, which stretches across Wisconsin to the St. Croix River.
source: National Park Service — Ice Age Trail FAQ

title: The Ice Age Trail Reaches the St. Croix Bluffs
summary: Interstate State Park on the St. Croix River is the western end of the Ice Age National Scenic Trail.
source: National Park Service — Ice Age Trail FAQ

title: Wisconsin’s Glaciers Left Giant Kettle Depressions
summary: The Ice Age Trail showcases kettles, depressions formed as buried blocks of glacial ice melted after the ice sheet retreated.
source: National Park Service — Ice Age Trail

title: Ridges of Rubble Mark the Glacier’s Edge
summary: The Ice Age Trail passes moraines—ridges of rock and sediment deposited along the edge of the former continental glacier.
source: National Park Service — Ice Age Trail

title: A Glacial Landscape of Drumlins and Eskers
summary: The Ice Age Trail highlights drumlins, streamlined hills molded by moving ice, and eskers, winding ridges left by streams beneath glaciers.
source: National Park Service — Ice Age Trail
location: Eastern Wisconsin glacial landscape — representative point

title: Old-Growth Pine Crowns a Sandstone Mound
summary: Roche-A-Cri Mound State Natural Area contains old-growth pine and oak on sandy ground and rocky slopes surrounding its striking sandstone mesa.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Roche-A-Cri State Park — Nature

title: The Wisconsin River Has a 92-Mile Free-Flowing Corridor
summary: The Lower Wisconsin State Riverway protects a 92.3-mile free-flowing stretch from the Prairie du Sac dam to the Mississippi River, with sandbars, wooded banks and broad floodplain habitat.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Wisconsin River Water Detail

title: A Dam Marks the Start of the Lower Wisconsin Riverway
summary: Below the Prairie du Sac dam, the Wisconsin River runs without another main-stem dam all the way to its meeting with the Mississippi. The contrast with the dammed upper river is striking.
source: Wisconsin DNR — Wisconsin River Water Detail

title: Petenwell Is Wisconsin’s Second-Largest Lake
summary: Petenwell Lake is a Wisconsin River impoundment and the state’s second-largest inland lake. A hydroelectric dam controls its water level.

title: Petenwell’s Hydroelectric Dam Holds Back a Vast Flowage
summary: Petenwell’s power dam creates a 42-foot hydraulic head and regulates a vast Wisconsin River flowage that supports fishing and boating.

title: Castle Rock’s Blue-Green Algae Problem Has a Long History
summary: DNR monitoring in the 1990s documented heavy algal blooms and occasional low dissolved oxygen in Castle Rock Flowage, reflecting nutrient pressures in the watershed.

title: The First Wisconsin Dam Powered a Fox River Sawmill
summary: Wisconsin’s first documented dam was built at De Pere in 1809 to supply power to a sawmill on the Fox River, beginning a long era of millponds and river engineering.
source: Wisconsin DNR — History of Dams in Wisconsin

title: The Black River’s First Sawmill Changed Its Waters
summary: The first sawmill on the Black River dates to 1819. Early river dams created the waterpower and flowages that helped move Wisconsin’s lumber economy.
source: Wisconsin DNR — History of Dams in Wisconsin

title: A Territorial Law Allowed Mills to Flood Their Neighbors
summary: Wisconsin Territory’s 1840 Milldam Act encouraged water-powered mills by permitting dam owners to flood others’ land without first acquiring easements, setting off decades of disputes over river rights.
source: Wisconsin DNR — History of Dams in Wisconsin

title: Wisconsin Declared Navigable Rivers Public Highways
summary: In 1863, Wisconsin declared navigable waterways public highways. Later legal tests considered whether streams could float sawlogs, reflecting how important rivers were to transportation.
source: Wisconsin DNR — History of Dams in Wisconsin

title: Mirror Lake’s Sandstone Began as Ancient River Sand
summary: The sandstone cliffs around Mirror Lake formed from sand deposited by ancient rivers near shallow inland seas roughly 500 million years ago. Dell Creek later cut through the soft rock.

title: A Glacier Rerouted Dell Creek
summary: Geologists believe glacial outwash blocked Dell Creek’s former course, forcing it northeast into the channel now occupied by Mirror Lake and Lake Delton.

title: Dell Creek Makes a Sudden Right-Angle Turn
summary: Dell Creek bends sharply northeast near Reedsburg. Its unusual turn preserves clues to a much older drainage system altered by Ice Age deposits.

title: Mirror Lake’s Gorges Were Carved After the Ice Age
summary: Although the sandstone is hundreds of millions of years old, Dell Creek carved Mirror Lake’s steep gorges comparatively recently, during roughly the last 10,000 years.

title: The St. Croix Once Had a Giant Wooden Logging Dam
summary: Nevers Dam was built to control log drives on the St. Croix River. Its 614-foot wooden structure created a long flowage and helped prevent jams downstream at the Dalles.
source: National Park Service — St. Croix River Logging
location: Nevers Dam Landing, St. Croix River

title: Nevers Dam Used Electric Lights for Overnight Log Drives
summary: The Nevers logging dam had electric lights so crews could sluice timber through its gates around the clock during the height of the St. Croix lumber era.
source: National Park Service — St. Croix River Logging

title: The St. Croix’s Giant Logging Dam Disappeared
summary: Nevers Dam was removed in 1955, but surviving earthworks and former ice-breaker islands still hint at the enormous wooden structure that once controlled the river.
source: National Park Service — St. Croix River Logging

title: The St. Croix Once Had Hundreds of Logging Dams
summary: By the peak of the logging era, dozens of gated dams and hundreds of temporary splash dams regulated water across the St. Croix watershed to float pine logs toward mills.
source: National Park Service — St. Croix River Logging

title: An Early Log-Sorting Boom Stood Near Osceola
summary: The St. Croix Boom Company initially built a log-sorting boom near Osceola before moving its main operations downstream toward Stillwater to better serve sawmills and tributaries.
source: National Park Service — St. Croix River Logging

title: The Rock River Cut Through Horicon’s Natural Dam
summary: The Rock River gradually eroded a natural glacial moraine that had trapped meltwater in the Horicon basin, lowering the lake and allowing the marsh to develop.

title: Horicon Marsh’s Islands Are Buried Glacial Hills
summary: Many islands within Horicon Marsh are drumlins—streamlined hills left by glacier ice—partly buried beneath later wetland sediments.

title: A Rock River Dam Helps Restore Horicon Marsh
summary: After failed drainage schemes damaged Horicon Marsh, a dam on the Rock River helped restore its waters. Managers now adjust water levels to support diverse wetland habitats.

title: Horicon’s Water Levels Are Managed for Migrating Birds
summary: Wetland managers vary flooding and drawdowns at Horicon Marsh to mimic natural wet and dry cycles that support shorebirds, ducks and other marsh wildlife.

title: Three Streams Carved Wildcat Mountain’s Steep Valleys
summary: The Kickapoo River, Billings Creek and Cheyenne Creek cut winding, steep-sided valleys into the sandstone and dolomite around Wildcat Mountain.

title: Billings Creek Has a Waterfall That Freezes Into an Icicle
summary: Near Wildcat Mountain’s Ice Cave trail, a small spring spills over a sandstone ledge. In winter its flow can freeze into a large icicle against the rock.

title: Dell Creek Once Flowed Toward Baraboo
summary: Before Ice Age outwash reshaped local drainage, Dell Creek likely flowed southeast through a gap in the Baraboo Hills toward an older course of the Wisconsin River.

title: The Niagara Escarpment Rises Above Lake Winnebago
summary: At High Cliff State Park, the exposed edge of the Niagara Escarpment forms a rocky ledge above Lake Winnebago. The same long bedrock ridge extends northeast through Door County and onward toward Niagara Falls.

title: A Cliff Forest Grows Among Fallen Limestone
summary: High Cliff Escarpment State Natural Area protects wooded talus slopes, where limestone broken from the cliff creates rocky habitat for hardwood trees, ferns and spring wildflowers.
location: High Cliff State Park, Calumet County, Wisconsin

title: Ancient Effigy Mounds Overlook Winnebago
summary: Conical and animal-shaped effigy mounds survive in the woods above the escarpment at High Cliff. They are part of a much older Indigenous cultural landscape that predates the park.
location: High Cliff State Park, Calumet County, Wisconsin

title: Door County Bluffs Were Once a Seafloor
summary: Peninsula State Park’s dramatic dolostone bluffs belong to the Niagara Escarpment. Their rock originated as marine sediment hundreds of millions of years ago, long before the Door Peninsula existed.
location: Peninsula State Park, Door County, Wisconsin

title: A Rare Beech-Maple Forest Survives on the Peninsula
summary: Peninsula State Park protects a beech-maple forest as one of its two designated state natural areas, preserving a native woodland community amid a heavily visited Door County landscape.
location: Peninsula State Park, Door County, Wisconsin

title: White Cedars Cling to Door County Cliffs
summary: The White Cedar Forest State Natural Area protects a distinctive forest within Peninsula State Park, where rocky terrain and Lake Michigan’s influence help shape the vegetation.
location: Peninsula State Park, Door County, Wisconsin

title: A Dune Boardwalk Protects a Fragile Lakeshore
summary: Kohler-Andrae State Park’s Dunes Cordwalk lets visitors cross the sand-dune landscape while limiting trampling of specialized dune plants along Lake Michigan.
location: Kohler-Andrae State Park, Sheboygan County, Wisconsin

title: Hundreds of Plant Species Grow Beside the Dunes
summary: More than 400 plant species have been recorded at Kohler-Andrae State Park. Its dunes support specialized vegetation, while wetlands and wooded areas add to the park’s botanical diversity.
location: Kohler-Andrae State Park, Sheboygan County, Wisconsin

title: A Great Lakes Flyway Passes Over the Sand Dunes
summary: Lake Michigan’s shore acts as a migration corridor at Kohler-Andrae. More than 150 bird species have been recorded in or passing through the park, from diving ducks to hawks and songbirds.
location: Kohler-Andrae State Park, Sheboygan County, Wisconsin

title: A White Cedar Swamp Hides Behind the Beach
summary: Beyond Harrington Beach State Park’s Lake Michigan shoreline, a white cedar and hardwood swamp shelters spring wildflowers and a very different habitat from the open beach.
location: Harrington Beach State Park, Ozaukee County, Wisconsin

title: Monarchs Gather Before Their Long Migration
summary: In late summer, monarch butterflies gather in the open fields at Harrington Beach State Park before their fall migration. Goldenrod and asters bloom around the same time.
location: Harrington Beach State Park, Ozaukee County, Wisconsin

title: The Quartzite Bluffs Tower Over Devil’s Lake
summary: At Devil’s Lake State Park, towering quartzite bluffs rise about 500 feet above the lake. The rugged rock landscape is one of the park’s defining geological features.
location: Devil’s Lake State Park, Sauk County, Wisconsin

title: An Oak Forest Survives Between Lake and Bluff
summary: Devil’s Lake Oak Forest is a designated state natural area between the park’s South Shore and group campground, protecting an important native woodland community.
location: Devil’s Lake State Park, Sauk County, Wisconsin

title: An Extraordinary Number of Plants Grow at Devil’s Lake
summary: Wisconsin DNR reports roughly 880 plant species in Devil’s Lake State Park, a reflection of its varied cliffs, forests, prairies and lakeside habitats.
location: Devil’s Lake State Park, Sauk County, Wisconsin

title: The Driftless Hills Hide a Five-Thousand-Acre Park
summary: Governor Dodge State Park protects more than 5,000 acres of steep hills, bluffs and deep valleys in southwestern Wisconsin’s Driftless Area, a landscape unlike the glaciated terrain farther east.
location: Governor Dodge State Park, Iowa County, Wisconsin

title: Horse Trails Wind Through the Driftless Bluffs
summary: Governor Dodge State Park offers horseback riding as well as hiking and biking across its rugged hills and valleys, giving visitors several ways to explore the Driftless landscape.
location: Governor Dodge State Park, Iowa County, Wisconsin

title: The Kickapoo Valley Has a Mountain Overlook
summary: Wildcat Mountain State Park sits high above the winding Kickapoo River. Its observation point opens a view across the valley and the steep ridges of Wisconsin’s Driftless Area.
location: Wildcat Mountain State Park, Vernon County, Wisconsin

title: A Virgin Hemlock Forest Survived on Mount Pisgah
summary: Cool north-facing cliffs at Mount Pisgah support pine and hemlock more typical of northern Wisconsin. The timber escaped logging and grazing, helping earn the area state natural area protection in 1952.
location: Wildcat Mountain State Park, Vernon County, Wisconsin

title: The Fern That Walks Across Wisconsin Cliffs
summary: Walking fern grows on shaded rock faces at Wildcat Mountain. When the tip of one of its arching leaves touches the ground, it can root and form another plant, giving the fern its unusual name.
location: Wildcat Mountain State Park, Vernon County, Wisconsin

title: Twenty-One Miles of Trails Cross Wildcat Mountain
summary: Wildcat Mountain State Park has 21 miles of hiking, nature and equestrian trails winding through ridges, wooded slopes and valleys above the Kickapoo River.
location: Wildcat Mountain State Park, Vernon County, Wisconsin

title: A Mississippi Bluff Park Links to a Rail Trail
summary: From Perrot State Park’s campground, cyclists can connect directly to the 24-mile Great River State Trail, which follows the Mississippi River corridor through western Wisconsin.
location: Perrot State Park, Trempealeau County, Wisconsin

title: Dragonflies Patrol the Trempealeau Wetlands
summary: Perrot State Park’s river wetlands shelter beavers, muskrats and mink. In warmer months, dragonflies and damselflies patrol the water and nearby prairies.
location: Perrot State Park, Trempealeau County, Wisconsin

title: A Hidden Prairie Grows Above a Sandstone Shelter
summary: The ridges near Natural Bridge State Park’s sandstone formation hold small native prairie remnants with grasses and even cacti, an unexpected contrast to the surrounding oak woods.
location: Natural Bridge State Park, Sauk County, Wisconsin

title: An Ice Age Shelter Preserved Lost Wildlife
summary: Excavations at Natural Bridge’s rock shelter recovered animal remains that include passenger pigeons, elk, wolves, fishers and other species, preserving evidence of Wisconsin’s changing wildlife.
location: Natural Bridge State Park, Sauk County, Wisconsin

title: A Nature Center Sits Among Lake Michigan Dunes
summary: Kohler-Andrae’s Sanderling Nature Center sits among the lakeshore dunes, with exhibits on local wildlife and access to trails that help visitors explore this fragile shoreline habitat.
location: Kohler-Andrae State Park, Sheboygan County, Wisconsin

title: The Namekagon Runs Tea-Brown Through the Northwoods
summary: Tannins from northern vegetation tint parts of the Namekagon River brown. Its forested banks form part of the federally protected St. Croix National Scenic Riverway.

title: Wild Rice Waves in Pacwawong Flowage
summary: The lake-like Pacwawong Flowage along the Namekagon supports wild rice, an important native aquatic plant of northern Wisconsin waterways.

title: Two Rivers Meet in the St. Croix Wilds
summary: The Kettle River joins the St. Croix near a stretch where the river divides around large islands and runs over rocky rapids.
location: St. Croix–Kettle River confluence, Burnett County, Wisconsin

title: The St. Croix Squeezes Through a Deep Rock Gorge
summary: Below the St. Croix Falls dam, the river enters the Dalles, a narrow rocky gorge with walls reaching roughly 70 to 100 feet in places.
location: St. Croix Dalles, Polk County, Wisconsin

title: Paddlers Can Follow the Baraboo River
summary: The Baraboo River is among Wisconsin waterways recognized by the DNR as a paddling route, connecting communities through the Baraboo Hills region.

title: The Flambeau Offers a Forest River Water Trail
summary: The Flambeau River State Forest includes mapped paddling routes through wooded northern Wisconsin, where river travel remains a way to experience remote forest landscapes.
location: Flambeau River State Forest, Price County, Wisconsin

title: The Brule River Runs Through a State Forest
summary: Wisconsin DNR identifies the Brule River State Forest as a destination for mapped water trails, linking paddlers with a northern river corridor.
location: Brule River State Forest, Douglas County, Wisconsin

title: The Peshtigo Has a Forest Water Trail
summary: The Governor Earl Peshtigo River State Forest includes water-trail opportunities along the Peshtigo River in northeastern Wisconsin.

title: A Water Trail Winds Around Brunet Island
summary: The Chippewa River and surrounding channels give the Cornell area a distinctive water landscape near Brunet Island State Park.

title: The Turtle-Flambeau Holds a Maze of Water
summary: The Turtle-Flambeau Scenic Waters Area is among Wisconsin DNR’s featured flowages for water-based recreation, with extensive wooded shoreline and islands.

title: Willow Flowage Offers a Northwoods Water Escape
summary: Willow Flowage Scenic Waters Area preserves a large water-and-forest landscape that the DNR highlights for paddling and other water recreation.

title: A Paddle Route Crosses the Chippewa Flowage
summary: The Chippewa Flowage is among Wisconsin’s featured paddling destinations, where connected bays and islands create many possible routes.

title: The Pine River Is Protected as a Wild River
summary: The Pine River is one of Wisconsin’s designated wild rivers, protected for its natural character and valued as a remote paddling destination.

title: The Popple Shares Wild River Protection
summary: The Popple River is protected alongside the Pine as one of Wisconsin’s wild rivers, preserving an undeveloped northern river corridor.

title: The Pike River Has Wild River Status
summary: The Pike is among Wisconsin’s designated wild rivers, recognized for its natural river landscape and paddling opportunities.

title: The Totagatic Remains a Wild River
summary: The Totagatic River is designated as a Wisconsin wild river, protecting a long northern waterway known for its relatively undeveloped setting.

title: Buckhorn Has a Marked Water Trail
summary: Buckhorn State Park offers mapped paddling routes along the Castle Rock Lake landscape, where sheltered water meets marsh and wooded shore.
location: Buckhorn State Park, Juneau County, Wisconsin

title: Paddlers Explore the Mouth of the Wisconsin River
summary: Wyalusing State Park sits near the meeting of the Wisconsin and Mississippi rivers and is among the parks listed by the DNR for mapped water trails.
location: Wyalusing State Park, Grant County, Wisconsin

title: Perrot State Park Has a Water Trail
summary: Perrot State Park provides a paddling setting among Mississippi River backwaters and the dramatic bluffs of the upper river valley.
location: Perrot State Park, Trempealeau County, Wisconsin

title: Big Bay Connects to the Superior Water Trail
summary: Big Bay State Park on Madeline Island connects visitors with Lake Superior paddling opportunities along Wisconsin’s Great Lakes water-trail network.
location: Big Bay State Park, Ashland County, Wisconsin

title: The Lower Wisconsin Has a Long Riverway
summary: The Lower Wisconsin State Riverway protects a broad river corridor valued for sandbars, floodplain habitat and paddling between Prairie du Sac and the Mississippi.
location: Lower Wisconsin River, Richland County, Wisconsin

title: Northern Highland Lakes Form a Paddling Landscape
summary: The Northern Highland-American Legion State Forest contains many interconnected lakes and waterways and is among DNR-listed water-trail destinations.
location: Northern Highland-American Legion State Forest, Vilas County, Wisconsin

title: A Water Trail Passes Through the St. Croix Bluffs
summary: The protected St. Croix River corridor combines broad water, wooded banks and rocky reaches as it travels toward the Mississippi.
location: St. Croix River, St. Croix County, Wisconsin

title: Wisconsin Has a Water Trail Along Lake Michigan
summary: Wisconsin’s Lake Michigan State Water Trail follows the state’s eastern shoreline, connecting coastal communities and paddling access points.
location: Lake Michigan shore, Manitowoc County, Wisconsin

title: The Apostle Islands Have Shoreline Hiking and Paddling
summary: The Apostle Islands combine island trails, beaches and Lake Superior waters; visitors reach many of the islands by boat and can explore designated hiking routes ashore.

title: Brooks Bluff Rises Above the Central Sands
summary: Brooks Bluff is among the protected natural areas of Adams County, preserving a distinctive upland feature in Wisconsin’s central landscape.

title: Quincy Bluff Protects Sand Country Wetlands
summary: Quincy Bluff and Wetlands is a protected natural area combining a prominent bluff with wetlands in Adams County.
location: Quincy Bluff and Wetlands, Adams County, Wisconsin

title: A Rare Fen Survives at French Creek
summary: French Creek Fen is a designated natural area in Columbia County, preserving a wetland habitat in the south-central Wisconsin landscape.
location: French Creek Fen, Columbia County, Wisconsin

title: Gibraltar Rock Overlooks the Wisconsin Countryside
summary: Gibraltar Rock is a protected natural area in Columbia County where a prominent rock outcrop rises above the surrounding countryside.

title: A Pine Savanna Survives on an Ancient River Plain
summary: Pine Island Savanna is a protected natural area in Columbia County, conserving a landscape shaped by sandy soils and open woodland.
location: Pine Island Savanna, Columbia County, Wisconsin

title: A Driftless Ridge Shelters Hogback Prairie
summary: Hogback Prairie is a designated Crawford County natural area, protecting prairie vegetation on a ridge in the Driftless landscape.

title: Kickapoo Wild Woods Protects a Driftless Forest
summary: Kickapoo Wild Woods is a protected natural area in Crawford County, conserving forest habitat in Wisconsin’s rugged southwest.
location: Kickapoo Wild Woods, Crawford County, Wisconsin

title: Rush Creek Bluffs Shelter Prairie Habitat
summary: Rush Creek is a protected natural area in Crawford County, part of the bluff-and-prairie landscape along Wisconsin’s western border.

title: Cherokee Marsh Preserves a Wetland Near Madison
summary: Cherokee Marsh is a designated natural area in Dane County, protecting wetland habitat near the Yahara River system.

title: Goose Lake Drumlins Preserve Glacial Landforms
summary: Goose Lake Drumlins is a protected natural area in Dane County named for the streamlined hills left by glacial activity.
location: Goose Lake Drumlins, Dane County, Wisconsin

title: A Bog Hides Near Hook Lake
summary: Hook Lake Bog is a designated Dane County natural area that protects a wetland community distinct from the surrounding agricultural landscape.
location: Hook Lake Bog, Dane County, Wisconsin

title: An Oak Savanna Survives at Mazomanie
summary: Mazomanie Oak Barrens is a protected natural area preserving an open oak landscape in the lower Wisconsin River region.
location: Mazomanie Oak Barrens, Dane County, Wisconsin

title: Scuppernong Prairie Protects Open Grassland
summary: Scuppernong Prairie is a designated natural area in Waukesha County, protecting prairie habitat within southeastern Wisconsin.

title: A Prairie Thrives on Smith Drumlin
summary: Smith Drumlin Prairie protects native prairie on a glacial hill in Dane County, bringing two distinctive Wisconsin landscapes together.
location: Smith Drumlin Prairie, Dane County, Wisconsin

title: Thunder Mountain Is a Protected Northern Landmark
summary: Thunder Mountain is a designated natural area in northeastern Wisconsin, preserving a prominent upland landscape.

title: Enterprise Hemlocks Shelter a Northwoods Forest
summary: Enterprise Hemlocks is a designated natural area in Oneida County, conserving northern forest habitat associated with mature hemlock trees.

title: A Northern Pine Forest Grows Along the Tomahawk
summary: Lower Tomahawk River Pines is a protected natural area in Oneida County, conserving pine forest along a northern Wisconsin river.
location: Lower Tomahawk River Pines, Oneida County, Wisconsin

title: Wind Pudding Lake Has a Protected Shoreline
summary: Wind Pudding Lake is among Oneida County’s designated natural areas, protecting a northern lake landscape and its surrounding habitats.
location: Wind Pudding Lake, Oneida County, Wisconsin

title: A Spring-Fed Landscape Survives at Mecan Springs
summary: Mecan Springs is a designated natural area in Waushara County, protecting habitat around the headwaters of a central Wisconsin trout-stream landscape.

title: Karner Blue Meadow Preserves Rare Habitat
summary: Karner Blue Meadow is a protected natural area in Waushara County, named for the endangered butterfly associated with Wisconsin’s sandy barrens.

title: Powers Bluff Protects a Maple Forest
summary: Powers Bluff Maple Woods is a designated natural area in Wood County, preserving forest on one of central Wisconsin’s distinctive uplands.
location: Powers Bluff Maple Woods, Wood County, Wisconsin

title: A Tamarack Forest Survives at Hog Island
summary: Hog Island Tamaracks is a protected natural area in Wood County, conserving a wet forest landscape dominated in part by tamarack.
location: Hog Island Tamaracks, Wood County, Wisconsin

title: A Bog Forest Survives in the Mead Landscape
summary: Mead Conifer Bogs is a designated natural area in Wood County, protecting wet conifer habitat within central Wisconsin.
location: Mead Conifer Bogs, Wood County, Wisconsin

title: The Apostle Islands Have a High Lake Overlook
summary: An overlook trail on Stockton Island leads to a viewpoint high above Lake Superior, with views across the Apostle Islands.

title: A Fragile Sandspit Has Its Own Island Trail
summary: Stockton Island’s Sandspit Trail follows the shoreline near a delicate plant community; visitors are directed to established paths and boardwalks.

title: The Namekagon Changes From Rock to Sand
summary: The Namekagon generally runs shallow over a rocky bottom in its upper reaches. Near its meeting with the St. Croix, the riverbed becomes sandier—a change paddlers can notice as they travel downstream.

title: Hayward and Trego Dams Require a Portage
summary: Two working dams interrupt paddling on the Namekagon: one at Hayward and another at Trego. The National Park Service directs paddlers to portage around both structures.

title: The Upper Namekagon Shelters Cold-Water Trout
summary: The colder upper Namekagon supports brook and brown trout, particularly upstream from Larson Road Landing. Farther downstream, the river changes character as its water warms.
location: Upper Namekagon River, Sawyer County, Wisconsin

title: Old Logging Dams Still Shape Namekagon Rapids
summary: The Namekagon still carries traces of its logging past. Former dam sites at Phipps and Pacwawong create changes in the current; some can be run by paddlers when water is high enough.

title: The Namekagon Braids Around Forest Islands
summary: The Namekagon winds through forested country, splitting into braided channels around small islands in some stretches. Its twisting route gives paddlers a very different experience from a broad open lake.

title: A Hidden Portage Linked Two Wisconsin Watersheds
summary: A historic portage connected the Namekagon watershed with Lake Courte Oreilles and the Chippewa River system. Ojibwe travelers and later explorers used this route between major Wisconsin waterways.

title: Stinnett Dam Left Turbulence Behind
summary: Although the old Stinnett logging dam is gone, the National Park Service documents turbulent water at the former gate and altered banks nearby—physical reminders of the river’s timber-driving era.

title: The Veazie Dam Left Its Anchors on the Shore
summary: From the Trego Nature Trail, visitors can see where the former Veazie Dam was anchored to the Namekagon’s bank. The surviving landscape marks a chapter in Wisconsin’s logging history.

title: The St. Croix Hides Rare Freshwater Mussels
summary: The St. Croix–Namekagon system supports unusually diverse freshwater mussels, including federally listed species. These animals filter river water and depend on connected, healthy aquatic habitat.

title: Glacial Lake Duluth Helped Carve the St. Croix Dalles
summary: Torrential meltwater released from glacial Lake Duluth helped expose and erode the ancient basalt at the St. Croix Dalles, leaving a steep gorge visible along the Wisconsin–Minnesota border.
location: St. Croix Dalles, St. Croix Falls, Wisconsin

title: The St. Croix Becomes a Lake Above the Falls
summary: A hydroelectric dam at St. Croix Falls backs up the river for roughly ten miles, creating a lake-like stretch of water before it plunges into the rocky Dalles downstream.
location: St. Croix River above St. Croix Falls, Wisconsin

title: Big Manitou Falls Drops 165 Feet

location: Pattison State Park, Douglas County, Wisconsin

title: Little Manitou Falls Has Twin Cascades

location: Pattison State Park, Douglas County, Wisconsin

title: The Black River Gets Its Root-Beer Color From Plants

location: Black River, Pattison State Park, Wisconsin

title: The Douglas Fault Helped Create Amnicon Falls

location: Amnicon Falls State Park, Douglas County, Wisconsin

title: Copper Falls Sits Among Ancient Lava Flows

title: The Bad River Runs Through Copper Falls Gorge

location: Bad River, Copper Falls State Park, Wisconsin
